title: VIT-DRN-OCAFF: An Optimized Cross-Attention Feature Fusion Framework for Multi- Class COVID-19 and Pulmonary Disease Diagnosis Using Thoracic CT Images
abstract: Abstract Early and accurate pulmonary disease diagnosis remains a major challenge due to the rising prevalence of respiratory infections and chronic lung disorders. The COVID-19 pandemic further emphasized the need for intelligent diagnostic frameworks capable of rapidly identifying pulmonary abnormalities from thoracic Computed Tomography (CT) images. This study proposes a novel Vision Transformer–Dilated Residual Network with Optimized Cross-Attention Feature Fusion (ViT-DRN-OCAFF) framework for multi-class pulmonary disease classification. The proposed architecture combines the global contextual learning capability of Vision Transformers with the lesion-sensitive feature extraction of Dilated Residual Networks, while the Optimized Cross-Attention Feature Fusion (OCAFF) mechanism adaptively refines and integrates complementary pulmonary representations. A comprehensive dataset containing 24,860 thoracic CT images collected from public repositories and collaborating clinical centers was utilized, comprising COVID-19, viral pneumonia, bacterial pneumonia, and non-viral lung abnormalities. Advanced preprocessing techniques, including lung segmentation, adaptive contrast enhancement, lesion-aware normalization, volumetric augmentation, and image refinement, were employed to improve diagnostic feature quality. The Vision Transformer branch captured long-range contextual pulmonary dependencies, whereas the Dilated Residual Network extracted fine-grained pathological features associated with pulmonary lesions. Subsequently, the OCAFF module dynamically prioritized discriminative pulmonary characteristics and minimized redundant activations for improved classification reliability. Experimental evaluation using a 70:15:15 training-validation-testing protocol demonstrated superior performance with 99.42% accuracy, 99.31% precision, 99.27% sensitivity, 99.48% specificity, and 99.29% F1-score, outperforming existing pulmonary disease classification techniques.

title: Assessment of Atrioventricular and Ventriculoarterial Coupling Indices in Patients with Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome Utilizing Cardiac MRI and Invasive Hemodynamics
abstract: Abstract Background Atrioventricular (AV) and ventriculoarterial (VA) coupling indices have demonstrated prognostic value in various cardiac pathologies but have not been studied in hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). This study assessed known and novel AV and VA coupling indices derived from cardiac MRI (CMR) and invasive hemodynamics for predicting adverse outcomes in HLHS patients with stage II palliation prior to Fontan completion. Methods CMR and catheterization data from 45 HLHS patients with stage II palliation undergoing pre-Fontan evaluation (January 2015–October 2025) were retrospectively analyzed. Known AV coupling indices and two novel indices—RA SV -RV coupling index (RA stroke volume indexed/RV end-diastolic volume indexed) and combined RA-RV-Aorta coupling index—were compared between patients with and without adverse outcomes (composite of death, transplantation, heart failure hospitalization, SGLT2 inhibitor initiation, plastic bronchitis, protein-losing enteropathy). Predictive performance was assessed using Firth logistic regression and ROC analysis. Results Ten patients (22%) experienced adverse outcomes. Known AV coupling indices did not significantly differ between groups (AUC 0.48–0.69). The RV-Aortic coupling index was significantly lower in the adverse outcomes group (0.17 vs. 0.23, p = 0.006; AUC = 0.80). Both novel indices demonstrated superior discrimination: RA SV -RV (0.11 vs. 0.17, p = 0.002; AUC = 0.82) and novel RAsv-RV-Aorta (2.13 vs. 3.90, p = 0.001; AUC = 0.86). Nested models showed that adding each novel index to RV-Aortic coupling significantly improved model fit (p = 0.036 and p = 0.048, respectively). Conclusions Novel coupling indices designed for single ventricle physiology outperformed known AV coupling indices and provided incremental predictive value beyond RV-Aortic coupling alone for adverse outcomes in HLHS patients with stage II palliation.

title: Primary Solitary Fibrous Tumor of the Lacrimal Sac Mimicking Lymphoma: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Primary solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) of the lacrimal sac is among the rarest presentations of this mesenchymal neoplasm. We report a patient in whom the mass was initially dismissed as chronic dacryocystitis during three months of conservative therapy, and an outside magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) report suggested lymphoma. The diagnosis was ultimately resolved by signal transducer and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6) immunohistochemistry performed on the resected tissue. Case presentation: A 50-year-old Chinese man was referred with a two-year history of a painless, slowly growing right medial canthal mass. After three months of unsuccessful antibiotic and warm-compress therapy for presumed chronic dacryocystitis at another hospital, imaging raised concern for lymphoma. title: Correlation Between Demographic Data and Intraoperative Distal Femoral Anthropometry in Patients Undergoing Total Knee Arthroplasty
abstract: Abstract Background : Accurate prediction of femoral component size is important, particularly in populations with diverse anthropometry. Radiographic templating is resource-intensive. Demographic parameters may offer a simple alternative, but data from African populations are scarce. Objectives: To determine the correlation between demographic data and intraoperative distal femoral anthropometric measurements in patients undergoing primary total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Methods : This cross-sectional study included 78 consecutive patients undergoing primary TKA for osteoarthritis at a regional Orthopaedic Hospital in Nigeria between May 2024 and April 2025. Preoperative age, sex, height, weight and BMI were recorded. Intraoperatively, anteroposterior diameter (fAPD) and mediolateral width (fMLW) of the resected distal femur were measured using a Vernier caliper. Pearson correlation and multivariate linear regression were performed using SPSS v28. Results : Mean age was 66.12 ± 6.30 years. Mean fAPD was 58.65 ± 5.95 mm and fMLW was 70.11 ± 6.91 mm. Female sex predicted both fAPD [B = -4.801, β = -.283, p =.021] and fMLW [B = -8.310, β = -.420, p <.001]. Height predicted fAPD [B = 139.245, β = 1.760, p =.045], and age independently predicted fMLW [B = -.230, β = -.210, p =.028]. The fAPD model was significant [F (5,72) = 3.84, p =.004, R² = 0.211]. The fMLW model was significant [F (5,72) = 8.10, p <.001, R² = 0.428]. Weight and BMI were not significant predictors. Conclusion: In this Nigerian cohort, intraoperative distal femoral dimensions were primarily determined by sex, with additional contributions from height for APD and age for MLW. These findings support consideration of sex, age, and height in preoperative planning for TKA. Level of Evidence: III

title: Quadratus Lumborum Block for Robotic Prostatectomy: Improved Early Recovery but Not Short-Term Event-Free Survival — A Randomized Trial
abstract: Abstract Objective : This randomized, double-blind trial investigated whether adding a quadratus lumborum block (QLB) to general anesthesia (GA) improves 6‑month event‑free survival (EFS) and recovery after robot‑assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy (RALP). Methods : Three hundred fifty patients were randomized; the modified intention-to-treat population comprised 299 patients (GA+QLB, n=148; GA alone, n=151). The primary outcome was 6‑month EFS (composite of biochemical/radiographic recurrence or initiation of salvage/adjuvant therapy). Secondary outcomes included opioid consumption, pain scores, quality of recovery, and inflammatory markers. Results : Baseline characteristics were available for the per-protocol population (n=286). Within the confines of this trial, we did not detect a statistically significant difference in 6-month EFS between the GA+QLB and GA groups (adjusted HR = 0.858, 95% CI: 0.572–1.285, P = 0.457). However, the GA+QLB group demonstrated clinically meaningful improvements in early recovery outcomes, including significantly lower intraoperative opioid consumption, lower postoperative pain scores, shorter time to first flatus, and higher QoR‑40 scores on postoperative day 1 (all P < 0.05). Inflammatory and immune markers showed no significant intergroup differences. Conclusion : In this randomized trial, adding QLB to GA did not improve the 6‑month composite EFS endpoint for RALP. While the oncologic effect remains inconclusive and requires longer follow‑up, the study provides robust evidence that QLB significantly enhances early recovery—reducing opioid use and improving patient‑reported quality of recovery. These benefits support routine inclusion of QLB in multimodal analgesia for RALP within ERAS pathways. Trial registration : Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR); Identifier: [ChiCTR-2200066968]; Date of registration: December 22, 2022; Prospectively registered.

title: Cross-Scale Micro-CT Super-Resolution for Digital Rock Reconstruction in Heterogeneous Conglomerate Reservoirs
abstract: Abstract Accurate cross-scale characterization of heterogeneous reservoirs is needed for digital-rock analysis, hydrocarbon production, and subsurface energy storage assessment. Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) faces a field-of-view-resolution trade-off: large-volume scans capture gravel-scale heterogeneity but miss pore-scale features. This study presents Hy-MambaIR, a hybrid Mamba-Transformer network for super-resolution reconstruction of micro-CT images from heterogeneous conglomerate reservoirs. A local-to-global serial architecture combines windowed self-attention and dynamic Tanh normalization for fine-pore recovery with Mamba-based global modeling and spatial-channel attention for large-scale gravel structures. The model was evaluated with paired multi-resolution micro-CT images and against representative convolutional and Transformer baselines. Hy-MambaIR achieved a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 33.36 dB, exceeding HAT by 1.31 dB, and reached 30 dB with 6.6-fold fewer training iterations than HAT. Physical validation showed that the reconstructed images preserved segmentation accuracy, pore topology, pore-throat distributions, and single-phase flow fields; the mean relative error of three-directional absolute permeability on the 855^3-voxel representative elementary volume was 18.56%. Supervised fine-tuning on pebbly sandstone reduced this MRE to 3.59%. These results establish a computational route for physically informed digital-rock reconstruction and reservoir characterization in heterogeneous geoenergy systems.

title: Comparing MiniDock MTB, chest radiography, and symptoms for tuberculosis screening: a community-based evaluation in Karachi, Pakistan
abstract: Abstract Background Community-based active case finding (ACF) for tuberculosis (TB) is constrained by limited access to chest X-ray (CXR) and reliance on sputum-based diagnostic testing. Recently, WHO recommended near point-of-care testing which offers a non-sputum alternative, tongue swab (TS). We evaluated the feasibility and screening performance of MiniDock MTB on TS compared with WHO four-symptom screening (W4SS) and CXR in Pakistan. Methods We conducted 49 screening camps in underserved communities of Karachi. All adolescents and adults (> 10 years) underwent screening via W4SS, CXR, and TS collection. Individuals screening positive by any method were asked to provide sputum for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra, sputum swab testing on MiniDock MTB, and mycobacterial culture. A microbiological reference standard (MRS) was defined as a positive Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra and/or mycobacterial culture. Results Overall, 4,303 individuals were screened (median age 28 years [IQR 16–40]); 38% were female. All participants had CXR and W4SS screening results, while 3,432 (79.8%) had valid TS results. Overall, 752 participants were screen-positive for TB, including 606 with valid TS results. TS was positive in 19/3,432 (0.4%), CXR in 302/4303 (7.0%) and W4SS in 522/4,303 (12.1%). Sputum was collected from 243 (32%) of 752 screen-positive participants, including 225 (37%) with valid TS results; Among 30 MRS-positive individuals, 29 had abnormal CXR, 14 had symptoms and 13 a positive TS result. CXR showed the highest sensitivity (96.7%; 95% CI 82.8–99.9), compared with W4SS (46.7%; 95% CI 28.3–65.7) and TS testing (46.4%; 95% CI 27.5–66.1). Conclusion TS testing, although feasible, was not sufficiently sensitive to function as a standalone TB screening test. Further optimization of specimen collection, assay performance, and evaluation in diverse settings is needed to better define the role of TS testing in community-based TB screening.

title: PSA Trends and Clinical Outcomes Following Radiotherapy Combined with Androgen Deprivation Therapy for Prostate Cancer: A Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study from Saudi Arabia
abstract: Abstract Background Combined external-beam radiotherapy and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is standard treatment for men with intermediate- to high-risk prostate cancer, but outcome data from the Gulf region remain limited despite a rising regional disease burden. We evaluated longitudinal PSA response, treatment-related morbidity, and oncological outcomes in patients treated with curative-intent radiotherapy plus ADT, characterising PSA kinetics over the first nine months of treatment and identifying clinical predictors of the PSA trajectory. Methods In this retrospective cohort study at King Abdulaziz Medical City, Riyadh, we included all adult patients with prostate cancer who received radiotherapy combined with ADT and had complete treatment and follow-up records. Demographic, clinical, and treatment data were extracted from electronic medical records, with serial PSA recorded at baseline and at 3, 6, and 9 months. Changes in PSA from baseline were assessed with the paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and a linear mixed-effects model (random intercept per patient; fixed effects for time, age, Gleason group, and metastatic status; PSA log₁₀[PSA + 1]-transformed) was used to identify predictors of longitudinal PSA levels. Results Seventy-four patients were included (median age 68.0 years, IQR: 63.0–75.0; median PSA at diagnosis 17.3 ng/mL, IQR: 9.3–33.0), 64.9% with Gleason group 4–5 disease. Most received hypofractionated radiotherapy (median 60 Gy in 20 fractions) with a single ADT cycle (90.4%), predominantly leuprolide (91.8%). PSA fell progressively at every interval (all p < 0.001): median reductions of 91.9%, 99.2%, and 99.7% from baseline at 3, 6, and 9 months, with the proportion achieving a ≥ 50% reduction rising from 73.2% to 93.0% over the same period; median PSA nadir was 0.028 ng/mL (IQR: 0.024–0.560). On adjusted mixed-effects modelling, reductions at each time point remained significant independent of age and Gleason group (β = −0.81 to − 1.13 versus baseline, all p < 0.001), while metastatic disease at presentation predicted higher longitudinal PSA levels. Disease recurrence occurred in 5.4% of patients, with a median time to recurrence of 68.5 months; treatment-related toxicity was low, with urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction each affecting fewer than 7% of patients at 12 months. Conclusions In this predominantly high-risk, real-world cohort, combined radiotherapy and ADT produced rapid, deep, and durable PSA suppression with low toxicity and low biochemical recurrence, irrespective of baseline Gleason grade. These findings support the effectiveness and tolerability of this regimen outside the trial setting and provide PSA kinetic benchmarks from an underrepresented population that may complement randomised evidence, though prospective data incorporating PSMA-PET-based surveillance are needed to confirm whether early deep response translates into durable survival benefit.

title: Deep Learning-Based Sex Classification and Chronological Age-Group Estimation from Knee Radiographs Using a Multi-Task Framework with Rank-Fusion and Tri-Loss Learning
abstract: Abstract The sex classification and chronological age-group estimation from the knee radiographs are a significant area of interest in forensic anthropology and clinical diagnostics. As the knee exhibits clear sexual dimorphism and predictable age-related morphological changes, knee radiographs provide a useful basis for demographic profiling. While most existing research focuses on pediatric maturation, relatively limited research has addressed automated, fine-grained frameworks for adult demographic assessment. This study proposes an automated, deep learning-based multi-task framework designed to extract demographic information from knee radiographs. The research is structured into two investigative tasks: Task 1 addresses sex classification through a Rank-Fusion Ensemble strategy, which combines the ranked predictions of multiple deep neural networks to identify sex-related morphological patterns. Task 2 focuses on chronological age-group estimation using a ConvNeXt-Tiny model. To capture the ordinal progression of chronological age groups, Task 2 utilizes a proposed Tri-Loss strategy that combines CORAL, Cross-Entropy, and Ordinal Regression loss functions. The results demonstrate promising performance for demographic estimation from knee radiographs. For sex classification, the Rank-Fusion Ensemble achieved an accuracy of 96.65% with an ROC-AUC of 0.9840. For chronological age-group estimation, the model reached a Top-1 accuracy of 71.29%. A detailed evaluation showed an ordinal MAE of 0.32 age-group intervals, suggesting that age-group predictions are largely aligned with adjacent categories, reflecting the ordinal and overlapping nature of age-related morphological variation in the knee. By utilizing knee radiographs as the primary imaging modality, the multi-task approach offers a quantitative alternative to traditional qualitative radiological observations in forensic and medical contexts.

title: ROI-Guided Lesion Segmentation for Maize Disease Phenotyping in Field Images
abstract: Abstract Accurate delineation of disease lesions in field images can support objective crop-health monitoring and image-based phenotyping of maize foliar diseases. However, variable illumination, cluttered backgrounds, and irregular lesion morphology can reduce the reliability of lesion segmentation in field conditions. This study evaluates whether the spatial quality of detector-generated regions of interest (ROIs) influences downstream lesion segmentation when the segmentation network is held constant. A two-stage framework was developed in which DT-YOLO localizes symptomatic regions before lesion delineation by a standard DeepLabV3 + network. DT-YOLO was derived from YOLOv11n by integrating C3k2_DualPConv blocks, post-neck Triplet Attention, and Minimum Point Distance Intersection over Union (MPDIoU) loss. The dataset included 4,126 original maize leaf images representing healthy leaves, gray leaf spot, northern leaf blight, common rust, and maize streak virus; augmentation expanded the detection dataset to 7,427 images. Pixel-level lesion masks were manually prepared for 600 images, and an independent set of 100 images was used for end-to-end evaluation. DT-YOLO achieved 89.0% mAP@0.5 with 2.52 M parameters and 6.40 GFLOPs. Although its mAP@0.5:0.95, precision, and recall were lower than those of YOLOv11n, DT-YOLO increased the ROI Alignment Score from 0.382 to 0.635. When coupled with the unchanged DeepLabV3 + model, it achieved 63.20% mIoU and 65.95% Dice, compared with 62.96% mIoU and 64.98% Dice for the YOLOv11n-based cascade. The modest downstream improvement indicates that ROI spatial alignment can affect lesion delineation, while also showing that localization errors remain a major limitation of end-to-end performance. This modular framework provides an approach for maize disease phenotyping and field-image analysis in which localization and lesion segmentation can be independently evaluated and improved.

title: Diagnosis and treatment of isolated tuberculosis of the posterior spinal elements: A retrospective study of 15 cases
abstract: Abstract Background Isolated tuberculosis (TB) of the posterior spinal elements is rare and often difficult to diagnose. We present the clinical features, diagnosis, treatment, and long-term outcomes of 15 patients with isolated posterior element TB. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 15 consecutive patients treated between October 2013 and January 2021. The patients’ baseline clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings were analyzed. The following outcomes were assessed: erythrocyte-sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), visual analogue scale (VAS) pain score, American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) grade, Kirkaldy-Willis functional grade, recurrence, and complications. Results The cohort included 7 male and 8 female patients, with a mean age of 32.9 ± 13.8 years. The diagnosis was supported by CT and MRI findings (all patients), positive T-SPOT results (13 patients), positive culture (8 patients), and histopathological confirmation (4 patients). Twelve patients required surgery, and 3 received conservative anti-TB therapy alone. The mean follow-up was 66.4 ± 4.4 months. ESR, CRP, and VAS scores decreased significantly after treatment. Among 9 patients with baseline neurological impairment, 8 improved by at least one ASIA grade; no patient deteriorated neurologically. No recurrence, vertebral body involvement, progressive kyphosis, implant failure, or deep infection was observed. Kirkaldy-Willis outcomes were excellent in 11 patients, good in 3, and fair in 1. Conclusion Isolated posterior element TB may be missed on plain radiographs. CT and MRI are essential for diagnosis. Anti-TB chemotherapy is fundamental, and surgery may be appropriate for selected patients with neurological deterioration, epidural abscess, sequestrum, large dorsal muscle abscess, or spinal instability.

Among 9 patients with baseline neurological impairment, 8 improved by at least one ASIA grade; no patient deteriorated neurologically. No recurrence, vertebral body involvement, progressive kyphosis, implant failure, or deep infection was observed. Kirkaldy-Willis outcomes were excellent in 11 patients, good in 3, and fair in 1. Conclusion Isolated posterior element TB may be missed on plain radiographs. CT and MRI are essential for diagnosis. Anti-TB chemotherapy is fundamental, and surgery may be appropriate for selected patients with neurological deterioration, epidural abscess, sequestrum, large dorsal muscle abscess, or spinal instability.

title: Regional Gray Matter Volume Differences and Clinical Correlates in Anorexia Nervosa
abstract: Abstract Objective Structural MRI findings in anorexia nervosa are widespread, but the regional pattern and its clinical and neurochemical meaning remain incompletely defined. Methods We analyzed T1 weighted MRI and clinical data from the BEACON and SCAN datasets, including 122 participants with anorexia nervosa and 128 healthy controls. Gray matter volume was extracted for 163 AAL3 regions and compared between groups with models adjusted for age, total intracranial volume and cohort. Within the anorexia nervosa group, partial Spearman correlations and restricted cubic splines assessed relationships of diagnosis selected regions with body mass index, eating disorder symptoms and affective symptoms. The pooled diagnostic contrast was also compared with 39 normative PET and SPECT maps across 148 AAL3 regions using spatial null permutations. Results Anorexia nervosa was associated with lower gray matter volume in the right olfactory cortex, left olfactory cortex and left inferior parietal gyrus. The adjusted differences were 0.0421, 0.0417 and 0.3209 mL in magnitude, with q values from 0.0210 to 0.0268. Effects had the same direction in both cohorts, although no region survived correction within either cohort alone. Partial rank correlations were not significant. Restricted cubic splines identified nonlinear associations of left inferior parietal volume with body mass index and dietary restraint. The diagnostic t map showed negative spatial correlations with normative mGluR5, SV2A, GABAa and 5 HT2A maps. Conclusion These results localize a reproducible structural pattern while separating diagnostic anatomy from clinical variation and normative neurochemical organization, providing specific targets for longitudinal and multimodal studies of anorexia nervosa.

title: County-Level Radiologist Workforce Density, Cancer Mortality, and the Modeled Impact of AI-Augmented Diagnostic Capacity: A U.S. Ecological Analysis
abstract: Abstract Timely cancer diagnosis depends on adequate diagnostic imaging capacity, yet radiologist workforce availability remains unevenly distributed across U.S. counties. This study examined the association between county-level diagnostic radiologist density and age-adjusted cancer mortality across 3,073 U.S. counties using cross-sectional ecological analysis integrating provider enrollment, cancer registry, socioeconomic, and population data. In the fully adjusted model, higher log-transformed radiologist density was significantly associated with lower cancer mortality (β = −2.01 per 100,000; 95% CI: −2.82 to − 1.19; p < 0.001), with results robust to spatial autocorrelation (spatial error model β = −1.96) and twelve sensitivity analyses. Counties with zero radiologist presence (n = 1,334; population 22.6 million) were identified as having the greatest modeled mortality burden. Decision-analytic scenario modeling estimated that AI-equivalent augmentation matching the median nonzero-county density (ΔAI = 6.05 per 100,000) would correspond to a modeled annual mortality difference equivalent to approximately 887 deaths in this subgroup. The modeled association showed diminishing marginal differences, with larger estimated differentials when capacity was introduced into zero-radiologist counties than in higher-density settings. These findings suggest radiologist workforce distribution may represent a policy-relevant marker of diagnostic capacity and highlight zero-radiologist counties as targets for further evaluation of capacity-expanding interventions, including AI-equivalent approaches.

title: Multisystem Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis Presenting with Spontaneous Pneumothorax and Osteolytic Lesions: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) is a rare myeloid neoplasm characterized by a highly heterogeneous clinical presentation, ranging from localized osseous lesions to multisystem disease involving high-risk organs. We report the case of a two-year-old girl who presented with persistent fever, dyspnea, and irritability. Initial chest radiography demonstrated a diffuse bilateral reticulonodular pulmonary pattern. During hospitalization, she developed a spontaneous right-sided pneumothorax associated with complete right lung atelectasis. Chest computed tomography revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary cystic lesions, while radiographs of the skull and long bones demonstrated multiple well-defined osteolytic lesions without periosteal reaction. The diagnosis of Langerhans cell histiocytosis was confirmed by histopathological examination. Despite intensive supportive management, the patient died seven days after admission because of severe pulmonary involvement. This case highlights the pivotal role of diagnostic imaging in the early recognition of multisystem LCH and underscores the importance of considering this entity in pediatric patients presenting with cystic lung disease accompanied by lytic bone lesions, as prompt diagnosis may facilitate appropriate management and improve clinical outcomes.

title: MCP-MedImg: Enabling Standardized PACS-AI Integration through the Model Context Protocol
abstract: Abstract Background: The proliferation of AI-assisted diagnostic models in medical imaging has created a fragmented integration landscape with PACS systems, leading to redundant development, inconsistent security compliance, and disconnected clinical workflows. Most AI diagnostic products exist as standalone Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), limiting scalability, auditability, and clinical adoption. Existing integration solutions (Direct Plugin, DICOM Router, VNA) are point-to-point adaptations without unified semantic layers. While the Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides tool invocation frameworks for AI agents, it lacks dedicated extensions for the medical imaging domain. Critically, global regulators (FDA, NMPA, EU) are converging on total product life cycle (TPLC) approaches demanding continuous post-market surveillance, yet no standardized protocol supports such surveillance at scale. Objective: We propose MCP-MedImg, an open reference architecture and protocol specification for interoperable integration and governance of AI services in medical imaging ecosystems, allowing AI capabilities to be discovered, invoked, monitored, and governed across heterogeneous healthcare environments without replacing existing PACS infrastructures. Methods: MCP-MedImg extends MCP with a four-layer architecture: Transport (DICOMweb-compatible, with dicom-mcp upward compatibility), Security and Compliance (PHI de-identification plus 14-column audit trail), AI Orchestration (model routing and version management), and Application Semantics (inspection-driven routing, lesion encoding, conditional human-in-the-loop verification). The specification defines six core information model entities and a tiered conformance model (five mandatory requirements, seven optional extensions). A reference implementation based on Orthanc PACS and nnU-Net validates protocol consistency, workflow, multi-model routing, DICOM SR/SEG generation, and audit trails. Results: The reference implementation demonstrated end-to-end interoperability, standardized service registration, structured result integration (DICOM SR/SEG), and auditable tracking of AI lifecycle events. On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 D, end-to-end latency under realistic clinical conditions was: LIDC-IDRI lung nodule CT (200 volumes, mean 5.4 s, P99 22.6 s) and MSD Heart cardiac MRI (10 volumes, mean 18.2 s, P99 27.6 s, 5-fold ensemble Dice 0.9324). Validation comprised 132 passing tests across 10 verification scenarios. Conclusions: MCP-MedImg aims to transform AI-assisted diagnosis from standalone software into auditable, service-oriented capabilities with conditional human-in-the-loop verification—directly addressing the regulatory surveillance gap and establishing foundations for governable public infrastructure in healthcare AI. By defining a tiered conformance model, the protocol enables incremental adoption: from minimal compliance (Level 1) through full production deployment (Level 3). The service-oriented delivery model, with built-in audit trails, configurable verification, and standardized output generation, significantly enhances clinical trust, lowers deployment barriers, and accelerates the adoption of AI-assisted diagnosis in routine clinical practice.

title: Resistance to thyroid hormone β (RTHβ) due to a THRB mutation (p.Arg429Gln) in a39-year-old woman initially treated for thyrotoxicosis
abstract: Abstract Background Resistance to thyroid hormone beta (RTHβ) is a rare inherited disorder characterised by elevated free thyroid hormone levels with non-suppressed or elevated TSH, most commonly caused by mutations in the THRB gene. The biochemical profile often mimics thyrotoxicosis or a TSH secreting pituitary adenoma, contributing to delayed or inappropriate treatment. Methods We describe the clinical course, biochemical findings and genetic analysis of a 39 year old woman who presented with palpitations, hypertension and elevated FT4 and FT3 despite a non-suppressed TSH, and who demonstrated no response to antithyroid medication. Genetic sequencing was performed. Results Initial testing showed normal TSH levels (2.45 mU/L), and elevated FT4 (29 pmol/L) and FT3 (7.6 pmol/L). Antithyroid therapy (Thiamazole) led to a paradoxal rise in TSH. Pituitary MRI was normal. Genetic analysis identified a heterozygous THRB gene variant, NM_001354712.2:c.1286G>A (p.Arg429Gln), classified as pathogenic. Antithyroid therapy was discontinued, and management was transitioned to betablockade. The patient remained clinically stable at a 24-months follow-up, and genetic counselling was initiated. Conclusion This case highlights that elevated FT4/FT3 with inappropriately normal or high TSH should raise suspicion of RTHβ. Genetic confirmation is critical to avoid unnecessary interventions and to guide appropriate long-term management and family screening.

title: A Case Report of a Giant Mucinous Cystadenoma Suspected to Be Associated with Ovarian Remnant Syndrome After Bilateral Adnexectomy: Diagnostic Pitfalls and Implications for Clinical Management.
abstract: Background Mucinous cystadenoma of the ovary is one of the common benign ovarian neoplasms. Nevertheless, when a huge pelvic mass develops years after bilateral adnexectomy, determining its tissue origin and establishing a differential diagnosis poses substantial challenges, complicating the clinical management of such secondary pelvic lesions. Case presentation This study reports a rare case of a giant pelvic mass occurring many years after bilateral adnexectomy in a 65-year-old Han Chinese female. Intraoperative exploration and postoperative histopathology confirmed the lesion as an ovarian mucinous cystadenoma, which was presumed to arise from residual ovarian tissue after previous surgery, consistent with ovarian remnant syndrome (ORS). However, the ovarian origin of this lesion was comprehensively determined based on prior surgical records, intraoperative findings, and histopathological morphology, without further confirmation by definitive immunohistochemical staining. Conclusion Ovarian remnant syndrome should be considered in the differential diagnosis of de novo pelvic masses following bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy. A review of prior surgical records is essential for tracing the origin of such lesions. For pelvic mucinous lesions, gastrointestinal and appendiceal origins should be prioritized for exclusion, accompanied by comprehensive characterization of pathological features. To minimize the risk of long-term postoperative lesions, complete resection of all ovarian tissue should be pursued during bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy in routine clinical practice.

title: Ultrasound Measurement of Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter for Detection of Elevated Intracranial Pressure in Pediatric Encephalitis.
abstract: Background and objectives Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) is a critical and potentially life-threatening complication of pediatric encephalitis. Early detection is essential for improved outcomes. This study assessed the diagnostic utility of optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) ultrasound for identifying elevated ICP in children with encephalitis. Methods A prospective descriptive case series was conducted at the Infectious Disease Intensive Care Unit (ID-ICU), Children's Hospital 1, Ho Chi Minh City, from August 2023 to April 2025. Children with encephalitis underwent daily ONSD ultrasound during the first seven days of admission. Elevated ICP was defined based on clinical signs and neuroimaging findings. ONSD measurements were compared between patients with and without elevated ICP, and age-specific diagnostic cut-off values were determined. Results Thirty-six patients were enrolled, with elevated ICP confirmed in 72.2% of cases. ONSD values were higher in patients with raised ICP than in those without at all time points. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis identified optimal ONSD thresholds for detecting elevated ICP of 5.2 mm in children younger than 60 months, 5.9 mm in those aged 60 months or older, and 5.6 mm in the overall cohort. Serial measurements showed a decline in ONSD over time. No significant difference was observed between right and left eye measurements, with strong inter-eye correlation. Conclusions Ultrasound measurement of ONSD is a useful, noninvasive, repeatable bedside tool for early identification of elevated ICP in pediatric encephalitis. Incorporating age-specific ROC-derived ONSD thresholds may improve diagnostic accuracy and support bedside assessment in pediatric intensive care settings.

title: The Incidence and Diagnosis of Intra-articular Extension With Spiral Distal Third Humerus Fractures.
abstract: Purpose Many orthopaedic injuries have associated fracture patterns that require specific diagnostic tests. The relationship between spiral distal humeral shaft fractures and intra-articular extension has not been previously assessed. The purpose of this study was therefore to identify whether there is an association between spiral distal humeral shaft fractures and intra-articular extension. Methods We conducted a retrospective review of patients with spiral distal third humeral shaft fractures (12A1, 12B1, and 12C1) from 2016 to 2021 at a single institution. We queried our electronic medical record using CPT codes (24500, 24505, 24515, and 24516) and ICD10 codes (S42.3 and S42.4). Inclusion criteria consisted of patients older than 17 years, spiral distal third humeral shaft fractures (12A1, 12B1, and 12C1), and patients with appropriate radiographic imaging. We recorded OTA fracture classification, presence of CT scan, and presence of intra-articular extension. Results Nine hundred seventeen patients were identified with humeral shaft fractures. Of those, 57 patients were included in the study with spiral distal third humerus fractures. One patient (1.8%) had intra-articular extension. Thirty patients had CT scans of the distal humerus; no additional cases of intra-articular extension beyond the single radiographically identified fracture were detected. Conclusion Distal third spiral humeral shaft fractures (AO/OTA 12A1, 12B1, and 12C1) rarely demonstrate intra-articular extension. In our cohort, only 1 case showed articular involvement and was apparent on initial radiographs. Therefore, routine CT imaging is not indicated for these fractures and should be reserved for patients with concerning clinical findings or radiographic features suggestive of intra-articular extension.

title: Lung ultrasound as part of a diagnostic algorithm to detect interstitial lung disease in rheumatoid arthritis patients at risk.
abstract: Objectives Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) affects 5-10% of patients with RA. While lung ultrasound (LUS) shows promise for RA-ILD detection, its role remains inconclusive. We aimed to assess its performance as a screening tool in at-risk RA patients. Methods We made a cross-sectional study of RA patients, including i) individuals >50 years old with ≥1 risk factor for ILD, and ii) patients with new-onset respiratory symptoms. All patients underwent clinical examination, pulmonary function testing (PFT), LUS, and chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT). LUS was considered abnormal in case of ≥5 total B-lines, and diagnostic accuracy was compared against HRCT, using a recent American Thoracic Society definition. Results We included 103 RA patients (73% women; mean age 63.4 years, median disease duration 7 years, 62% current or ever smokers, 68% seropositive for RF and/or ACPA). The majority (67 patients, 64.4%) reported no respiratory symptoms and had normal lung auscultation. According to ATS definition, 23 patients (22.3%) had ILD. Use of LUS for RA-ILD showed a sensitivity of 60.9% (95% CI: 40.8-77.8%), specificity of 63.7% (95% CI: 52.8-73.4%), and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 85% (95% CI: 73.9-91.9%). In regression and random forest analyses, LUS did not outperform DLCO for the prediction of RA-ILD. However, combination of negative LUS examination with normal DLCO essentially excluded RA-ILD (NPV 100%, 95%CI: 82-100%). Conclusions Negative LUS in combination with normal DLCO reliably exclude ILD in at-risk RA patients, supporting its role in early RA-ILD detection.

In regression and random forest analyses, LUS did not outperform DLCO for the prediction of RA-ILD. However, combination of negative LUS examination with normal DLCO essentially excluded RA-ILD (NPV 100%, 95%CI: 82-100%).

Conclusions

Negative LUS in combination with normal DLCO reliably exclude ILD in at-risk RA patients, supporting its role in early RA-ILD detection.

title: Design and Rationale of the APOLLO Registry: Integrated Assessment of Cardio-Renal Perfusion and Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Phenotyping Using 82Rb-PET/CT
abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome encompasses interconnected diseases that share pathophysiological mechanisms, including microvascular dysfunction. Although rubidium-82 positron emission tomography/computed tomography ({superscript 2}Rb-PET/CT) is routinely used for myocardial perfusion imaging, its potential for integrated cardio-renal perfusion assessment and broader CKM phenotyping remains underexplored. We recently developed a compartment modelling approach to quantify renal perfusion from existing routine cardiac 82Rb-PET/CT scans, enabling simultaneous assessment of myocardial and kidney perfusion. However, real-world registries integrating these phenotypes with clinical outcomes are lacking. AimTo establish a registry integrating 82Rb-PET-derived myocardial and renal perfusion, CT-derived CKM imaging biomarkers, and detailed clinical and outcome data. MethodsThe APOLLO registry is a single-centre, retrospective database comprising approximately 1,200 consecutive patients who underwent myocardial perfusion imaging with 82Rb-PET/CT at Alrijne Hospital (Leiderdorp, the Netherlands) between 2021-2023. Clinical, laboratory, medication, echocardiographic, and imaging data were retrospectively collected. Myocardial perfusion was quantified using myocardial blood flow and myocardial flow reserve, and renal perfusion using renal blood flow and effective renal plasma flow. Additional CT-derived biomarkers included measures of adiposity and frailty, great vessel diameters, and vascular calcification. Echocardiographic diastolic dysfunction grade, H2FPEF score, CKM stage, and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) were also collected. ConclusionThe APOLLO registry integrates {superscript 2}Rb-PET-derived myocardial and renal perfusion measurements with CT-derived CKM imaging biomarkers and clinical outcomes. This enables investigation of cardio-renal perfusion and their associations with CKM phenotypes and cardiovascular outcomes.

title: FERDINAND: An Open Framework for Download and AI-ready Preprocessing of IMPC 2D Radiographs
abstract: The International Mouse Phenotyping Consortium (IMPC) maintains a large archive of whole-body dorsoventral radiographs. However, heterogeneity in file formats, metadata completeness, orientation, and image quality limits its reuse for large-scale quantitative analysis. We present FERDINAND (Framework for Extracting and Restructuring Distributed IMPC radiographs into a Normalised, AI-ready Navigable Dataset), an open framework for programmatic access, harmonisation, quality control, and curation of IMPC radiographs. FERDINAND combines metadata retrieval and local radiograph archiving with centre-aware preprocessing, automated exposure screening, orientation standardisation, and clustering-assisted visual curation. Applied to IMPC Data Release 24, FERDINAND organises 104,819 radiographs acquired between February 2012 and June 2025 across ten phenotyping centres and 6,306 single-gene knockout mouse lines, with semi-automated curation recorded for every image. As an in-dependent validation of the harmonised output, a DeepLabCut-based bone-morphometry pipeline showed that FERDINAND-processed radiographs improve data efficiency for landmark detection: at reduced training-set sizes, they achieve better performance than original radiographs and require fewer manual annotations to reach a given level of quality. FERDINAND provides a reproducible foundation for artificial intelligence (AI)-ready analysis and scalable quantitative phenotyping of heterogeneous IMPC and comparable radiograph resources. The complete FERDINAND source code is openly available on GitHub.

title: Results of a Community-Based Coronary CT Angiography Screening in Asymptomatic Adults With Cardiovascular Risk Factors: The Broward County Heart Project
abstract: Background: Coronary CT angiography (CCTA) and calcium scoring detect subclinical coronary atherosclerosis, but the results of community based screening in asymptomatic adults with cardiovascular risk factors are poorly described. Objective. To describe the results of the first phase of a county-funded CT screening program and their variation by demographics, health system, time, and ZIP code. Methods. Retrospective analysis of aggregate reports from the Broward County Florida Heart Project (May 2023 to September 2025). Eligible residents were those with insurance coverage, age 45 to 70 years (limited exceptions), free of known cardiovascular disease and symptoms, with at least one risk factor. Examinations at six hospitals in four health systems were classified by the program team as normal (Category 1), abnormal (Category 2), or very abnormal (Category 3), with a separate flag for other non coronary abnormality. We used Wilson confidence intervals and chi square, trend, and Mantel Haenszel tests. Results. Among 7,135 participants (58.3% men; 79.0% White, 8.0% Black, 17.2% Hispanic), 43.2% had Category 1, 45.4% Category 2, and 11.4% Category 3 results; 56.8% (95% CI, 55.7% to 58.0%) had abnormal or very abnormal results. The proportion rose from 39.3% at 45 to 55 years to 78.5% at 71 or older (trend P<0.001) and was higher in men than women (68.9% vs 39.8%; odds ratio [OR], 3.36; 95% CI, 3.05 to 3.71). Rates were lower in Black than White participants (38.9% vs 58.6%; hospital adjusted OR, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.38 to 0.54) and in Hispanic than non Hispanic participants (51.0% vs 57.8%). Abnormal results ranged from 39.5% to 60.3% across health systems (P<0.001). Variation across the 50 highest volume ZIP codes did not exceed chance (P=0.53). Conclusions. More than half of insured, asymptomatic adults with risk factors screened in this community program had abnormal results, with steep age and sex gradients and unexplained variation across health systems. Black, Hispanic, and female residents were under-represented relative to the county

title: LuTuFlow: a deep learning-based pipeline for quantitative characterization of mouse lung tumors in CT imaging
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) is a widely used, non-invasive imaging tool to monitor tumor growth. Tumor identification and volumetric quantification are crucial for assessing tumor burden, whereas tracking individual tumors by aligning scans from multiple time points reveals disease progression. However, these processes remain largely dependent on manual analysis, limiting the accuracy, reproducibility, objectivity, and scalability of tumor characterization. Several deep learning models have enabled automated segmentation and object identification. However, open-source, integrated software platforms that cover the entire workflow – including processing raw CT images, annotating and tracking tumors through time, and generating data reports and visualizations – are still needed. Here, we present LuTuFlow, a computer vision pipeline incorporating a nnU-Net-based deep learning model, configured for murine lung segmentation and tumor analysis. We integrated these modules into a Napari plugin, allowing researchers to apply the entire automated workflow to transform raw CT scan datasets into quantitative readouts and interactive visualizations in a simple graphical user interface. The resulting model, iteratively refined using expert-corrected annotations, generated reliable quantitative estimates of tumor burden.

title: A Triple-Measure Model for Estimating Cranial–Brain Size Across Age Groups
abstract: Background Head circumference is widely used as an indirect indicator of brain growth and cranial capacity; however, its isolated use may lead to imprecise interpretations, particularly in borderline cases of microcephaly and megalencephaly. Complementary screening approaches that remain accessible and non-invasive may therefore be useful, especially in settings with limited access to neuroimaging. Objective To develop and evaluate an experimental, non-invasive model for estimating endocranial volume based on a combined cranial metric, termed the Triple-Measure, and to compare its performance with head circumference alone across different age ranges. Methods One hundred forensic facial approximations with known cranial scale were analyzed. Head circumference, sagittal arc, and coronal arc were measured on three-dimensional skull models, and their sum was defined as the Triple-Measure. Endocranial volume was obtained through direct segmentation of computed tomography data or by anatomical deformation of donor models. Regression analyses and validation procedures were performed, and the results were contextualized using literature-derived datasets to assess compatibility with established population parameters. Results The Triple-Measure showed a stronger correlation with endocranial volume (R = 0.83; R² = 0.69) than head circumference alone (R = 0.76; R² = 0.57), a difference confirmed by an F-test (F ≈ 17.03, p < 0.001). Validation analyses performed on independent CT cases demonstrated good agreement and consistency between predicted and measured values. The sample distribution was compatible with large population datasets derived from the literature. Based on these findings, an analog lookup table and a digital calculation tool were developed to support exploratory application across adult and developmental stages, with improved sensitivity in borderline situations. Conclusions The Triple-Measure may provide a more informative anthropometric proxy for endocranial volume than head circumference alone while remaining non-invasive and accessible. Given its exploratory nature, the method is best interpreted as a complementary screening approach intended to support clinical decision-making and to indicate when further imaging evaluation may be warranted. Additional studies with larger clinical datasets are recommended to refine its applicability across populations. Highlights Triple-measure shows improved association with endocranial volume compared to head circumference Proposed as a non-invasive, low-cost screening approach for micro- and megalencephaly Analog lookup table and digital calculator developed for exploratory and practical use Framework extended across neonatal, pediatric, and adult age groups using integrated datasets

title: Deep Learning and Radiomics Models for Predicting 90-Day Outcomes in Ischemic Stroke: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract: BackgroundAccurate prediction of 90-day outcomes following ischemic stroke is crucial for optimizing clinical strategies. This study aimed to systematically review and meta-analyze studies using deep learning (DL) and hand-crafted radiomics (HCR) models for predicting 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) outcomes after ischemic stroke. MethodsWe followed the PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews. Four databases (PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library) were searched comprehensively for studies published up to September 2025. Inclusion criteria encompassed original research focusing on ischemic stroke patients with mRS at 90 days as the primary outcome and predictive models utilizing imaging biomarkers from CT or MRI. Quality assessment of the included studies was conducted using the PROBAST and and METhodological RadiomICs Score (METRICS) tools. ResultsSeventeen studies were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. Models demonstrated good prognostic performance for 90-day outcomes, with pooled AUCs of 0.85 (95% CI: 0.80-0.86) for internal and 0.74 (95% CI: 0.67-0.89) for external validation sets, with no significant difference (p=0.42). Deep learning and hand-crafted radiomics models showed comparable diagnostic accuracy in the primary analysis (p=0.667); a difference in sensitivity favouring hand-crafted radiomics emerged only in a post-hoc analysis after exclusion of one outlier study. Models incorporating clinical variables significantly outperformed imaging-only models (p<0.01). CT- and MRI-based models showed similar performance. Treatment-specific analyses revealed higher sensitivity for IVT-based models and higher specificity for combined MT+IVT models. ConclusionsDL and HCR models demonstrate robust potential for predicting 90-day outcomes in ischemic stroke. Future research should focus on standardizing model evaluation metrics and incorporating explainable AI techniques to improve clinical applicability.

title: Instability as Signal: Diagnosing Latent Heterogeneity in Multimodal Survival Models
abstract: Multimodal deep learning models for cancer survival prediction frequently exhibit unstable and irreproducible performance, limiting their clinical applicability. Rather than proposing a new predictive architecture, this work presents a diagnostic investigation into the sources of this instability. Using a transformer-based deep fusion model combining RNA sequencing and histopathology data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort as a diagnostic probe, we demonstrate that global survival prediction is highly unstable across data splits. We then analyze the learned multimodal embeddings in an unsupervised manner, revealing stable latent patient subgroups with significantly divergent survival outcomes. These subgroups are not explained by canonical receptor status or immune infiltration, but instead align with tumor-intrinsic proliferative activity. Conditioning survival modeling on the largest discovered subgroup recovers strong and stable prognostic performance, substantially outperforming unimodal baselines. These findings indicate that survival predictability is conditional on latent heterogeneity and suggest that heterogeneity-aware modeling strategies are essential for robust multimodal prognostication. This work establishes a methodological framework for interpreting instability in multimodal survival learning.

title: Preoperative thymic output and T-cell repertoire diversity are associated with recurrence after nephrectomy for localized renal cell carcinoma
abstract: Radiographic thymic health and peripheral T-cell repertoire features have been linked to outcomes in renal cell carcinoma (RCC), but their prognostic value after curative-intent surgery is unclear. We quantified preoperative blood signal-joint T-cell receptor excision circles (sjTRECs), a marker of thymic output, in 218 patients with localized RCC undergoing nephrectomy and characterized T-cell receptor β (TCRβ) repertoires in 201 patients. We assessed overall survival (OS) and recurrence-free survival (RFS) using Kaplan-Meier and Cox models adjusted for age, sex, and Leibovich risk group. High sjTREC levels were associated with longer RFS after adjustment for age, sex, and Leibovich risk group (hazard ratio [HR] 0.50; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.29-0.87; p=0.015), with a concordant OS estimate (HR 0.62; 95% CI, 0.38-1.02; p=0.058). sjTREC provided additional prognostic information beyond Leibovich risk stratification for recurrence overall and among intermediate/high-risk patients (likelihood-ratio test, p=0.024 and p=0.034, respectively). Higher TCRβ diversity was associated with longer RFS overall (HR 0.76; 95% CI, 0.60-0.96; p=0.024) and among intermediate/high-risk patients with longer RFS (HR 0.71; 95% CI, 0.55-0.92; p=0.009) and OS (HR 0.80; 95% CI, 0.65-0.98; p=0.031). Preoperative sjTREC provided prognostic information beyond clinicopathological risk, with higher TCRβ diversity associated with favorable outcomes.

title: LightSuite: scalable atlas registration and cell detection across the central nervous system
abstract: ABSTRACT Deciphering brain-wide circuits requires large animal cohorts, yet computational bottlenecks in atlas registration and whole-volume cell detection reduce precision, reproducibility, and sample yield. We present LightSuite, an open-source framework enabling scalable, multimodal registration and cellular mapping across the central nervous system (CNS). LightSuite combines damage-resilient 3D point-cloud initialization with user-steerable non-rigid registration, and GPU-accelerated local background normalization for rapid, illumination-invariant cell detection. Applying LightSuite to Fos-dependent activity labeling in mice, we extracted reproducible, layer-resolved profiles of active cell density, soma-size distributions and per-animal labeling-efficiency factors. LightSuite computationally untwists and registers cleared spinal cords to map myeloarchitecture, reconstructs serial wide-field histology to map surface GluA1 distributions, resolves optic fiber tracks, and aligns in vivo functional ultrasound hemodynamics into common atlas coordinates. LightSuite establishes an integrated, accessible platform for cohort-level structural, molecular, and functional CNS mapping.

ABSTRACT

Deciphering brain-wide circuits requires large animal cohorts, yet computational bottlenecks in atlas registration and whole-volume cell detection reduce precision, reproducibility, and sample yield. We present LightSuite, an open-source framework enabling scalable, multimodal registration and cellular mapping across the central nervous system (CNS). LightSuite combines damage-resilient 3D point-cloud initialization with user-steerable non-rigid registration, and GPU-accelerated local background normalization for rapid, illumination-invariant cell detection. Applying LightSuite to Fos-dependent activity labeling in mice, we extracted reproducible, layer-resolved profiles of active cell density, soma-size distributions and per-animal labeling-efficiency factors. LightSuite computationally untwists and registers cleared spinal cords to map myeloarchitecture, reconstructs serial wide-field histology to map surface GluA1 distributions, resolves optic fiber tracks, and aligns in vivo functional ultrasound hemodynamics into common atlas coordinates. LightSuite establishes an integrated, accessible platform for cohort-level structural, molecular, and functional CNS mapping.

title: Gastric Glomus Tumor Mimicking a Neuroendocrine Tumor: A Case Report Highlighting Diagnostic Pitfalls.
abstract: Introduction Gastric glomus tumors (GGTs) are rare mesenchymal neoplasms arising from the modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus body. Their subepithelial location and pronounced hypervascularity overlap considerably with gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) and neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) on imaging and in small biopsy specimens, making an accurate preoperative diagnosis challenging; as a result, such lesions are frequently diagnosed after surgical resection. Case presentation A 38-year-old asymptomatic woman was found to have a 25-mm well-circumscribed, hypervascular submucosal lesion with a small central depression and minute ulceration in the upper gastric body during a routine health-screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) demonstrated a heterogeneous hypoechoic mass arising from the third sonographic layer without evidence of muscularis propria invasion. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a hypervascular lesion with no regional lymphadenopathy or distant metastasis. Conventional forceps biopsies targeting the minute ulceration, evaluated with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining alone, were interpreted as consistent with a NET, leading to a provisional diagnosis of a type III gastric NET. Because of the diagnostic uncertainty surrounding the NET diagnosis, and because the EUS and CT showed no evidence of deep or nodal spread, the patient underwent laparoscopic and endoscopic cooperative surgery (LECS) with a local full-thickness gastric resection rather than upfront gastrectomy with lymphadenectomy, and the defect was repaired through a protective mini-laparotomy. Definitive histopathology demonstrated uniform round-to-spindle cells arranged in a perivascular sheet pattern within a myxoid stroma. Immunohistochemistry (IHC) showed focal positivity for α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and negativity for KIT (CD117), CD34, chromogranin A, synaptophysin, desmin, and the S-100 protein, confirming a GGT. All surgical margins were negative, and no recurrence has been observed over 5 years of follow-up. Conclusions A GGT must be included in the differential diagnosis of hypervascular gastric subepithelial lesions (SELs), including those with a nested, NET-like architecture. H&E staining alone is insufficient for a definitive diagnosis; direct communication with the pathologist and comprehensive IHC profiling are indispensable. LECS is a favorable and effective organ-preserving strategy for localized gastric SELs when the diagnosis remains uncertain despite the preoperative evaluation.

title: Photoacoustic imaging of human brain function through intact adult skulls
abstract: Blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized noninvasive imaging of human brain function, but it indirectly senses deoxyhemoglobin through water-proton relaxation and relies on bulky, costly, noisy, enclosed, superconducting-magnet scanners. In contrast, photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) directly probes hemoglobin absorption using a more compact, lower-cost, quieter, open, magnet-free system. However, functional PACT of the adult human brain has so far been demonstrated only after surgical skull removal, because the skull strongly attenuates optical and acoustic signals. Here, we demonstrate non-invasive transcranial functional PACT (T-fPACT) through the intact adult skull. A densely packed, high-channel-count (3,072-element) hemispherical ultrasonic array provides near-$2π$-steradian simultaneous acquisition, enabling high sensitivity and single-shot three-dimensional imaging at 20 Hz that eliminates motion blurring. Participant-specific stabilization further enables measurement of small task-evoked hemodynamic responses over the entire task duration. In healthy adults, T-fPACT localized responses to expected sensorimotor regions, distinguished task-specific motor representations, and yielded consistent localizations across repeated task runs and visits. Comparison with high-field (7 T) fMRI showed spatially corresponding functional regions, while dual-wavelength imaging revealed distinct hemoglobin-weighted responses. These findings overcome the long-standing skull barrier in human brain PACT and establish non-invasive, rapid volumetric photoacoustic imaging of brain function.

title: SPARCL: Spatially Adaptive Regional Coverage for Active Learning in Chest X-ray Analysis
abstract: Pixel-level annotation for chest X-ray (CXR) lesion segmentation is expensive, making active learning (AL) essential. However, existing AL strategies fail to account for the spatial distribution of selected samples, resulting in inconsistent performance across focal (e.g., aortic calcification) and diffuse (e.g., nodules) pathologies. In this paper, we propose SPARCL (Spatially Adaptive Regional Coverage for Active Learning) to dynamically balance predictive uncertainty with cumulative spatial coverage. By employing a concave coverage function, SPARCL imposes diminishing returns on previously annotated regions, naturally directing the annotation budget toward under-labeled areas. Furthermore, an entropy gate reverts the algorithm to standard uncertainty sampling when spatial variation is absent. This coverage objective is monotone submodular, guaranteeing near-optimal greedy batch selection. To address how aggregate metrics like Dice obscure regional failures, we further introduce two metrics---Spatial Inconsistency (SI) and Performance Coverage (PC)---to quantify anatomical fairness across AL rounds. Evaluated on an in-house calcification cohort and public CXR benchmarks, SPARCL reaches 95% of fully supervised performance using only 24% of the data, compared to 29% for the best baseline. Ultimately, SPARCL ensures robust spatial reliability, surfacing regional gains that aggregate metrics miss.

title: HierarchiRetina: A Diabetic Retinopathy Screening and Grading Cascade with Heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts Lesion Segmentation
abstract: Clinical screening for diabetic retinopathy proceeds in stages, yet most automated systems grade fundus images with a single black-box network. Three gaps remain: (i) lesions differ widely in size and contrast, but segmenters typically apply the same blocks to all; (ii) ungradable images are usually excluded or treated as an extra class, and lesion-aware graders seldom test whether lesions drive the grade; (iii) staged systems often report each stage only on the images reaching it, leaving propagated errors unmeasured. HierarchiRetina, a screening, segmentation and grading cascade with inspectable stage outputs, addresses each gap. First, HSMoE-AUNet is a U-Net whose skip, bottleneck and decoder blocks are sparse mixtures of heterogeneous experts, with lesion-matched types, counts and losses; SwinHRUNetPP, a dual-encoder vessel segmenter, uses a field-of-view-restricted loss. Second, LG-DRG separates gradability from ordinal severity and lets lesion masks query the image through gated cross-attention. Third, an end-to-end evaluation counts screening misses as errors and traces each error to its stage. Pooled Dice ranged from 0.184 (microaneurysms) to 0.579 (exudates); vessel Dice was 0.731. On 58,689 held-out images from six datasets, end-to-end quadratic weighted kappa was 0.804, with referral sensitivity 0.832 at specificity 0.947, and the screening gate caused 66% of errors. In ablations, the grade ignored the masks, even with the cross-attention gate started open. On all 4,105 official DDR test images, six-class accuracy was 85.6%, above the best published six-class result we found (83.8%). Staged screening systems should be evaluated end-to-end, with stage attribution and mask ablation, before clinical deployment.

title: AI-Enhanced Hyperspectral Imaging for Intraoperative Detection of Low-Grade Glioma: A Clinical Study
abstract: Current image-guided neuronavigation techniques, such as intraoperative MRI and ultrasound, are limited by high costs, limited sensitivity and operational complexity. There is a clear need for more efficient systems to enhance intra-operative tumor detection and improve patient outcomes for intrinsic brain tumor resection. Whereas previous intraoperative brain HSI studies have predominantly investigated high-grade gliomas, glioblastomas, or mixed-grade cohorts, this clinical study focuses specifically on low-grade gliomas (LGGs). LGGs strongly resemble normal brain under white light conditions on the operative microscope. This study characterizes spectral differences between healthy and tumor tissue and provides a paired comparison of HSI- and RGB-based classification at matched tissue locations and under identical patient-level data splits. Tumor regions showed consistently lower reflectance, which may be associated with differences in hemoglobin concentration and oxygenation. A range of classification models was evaluated. The 3D CNN, which integrates spectral and spatial features, achieved the highest median ROC-AUC of 74.5%, compared with 67.9% for the spectral-only XGBoost model and 64.0% for the RGB-based model. These results support further investigation of HSI for low-grade glioma classification and quantify its performance relative to conventional RGB imaging in this cohort.

title: FETALFusion: Resolution-Aware State-Space Modeling for Multi-Domain Fetal Head Segmentation
abstract: Head circumference (HC) measured from 2D ultrasound is a routine marker of fetal growth, and automating it needs segmentations whose boundaries hold up on individual scans, not only on average. We present FETALFusion, a dual-path CNN-Mamba encoder-decoder for fetal head segmentation across acquisition types. It applies four-directional state-space scans only at the two highest-resolution stages, routes bottleneck features through domain-specific channel gates that are averaged at test time, and adds a weak landmark shape prior. We train jointly on transabdominal (HC-18) and transperineal (PSFHS) images and compare ten methods on a held-out test set of 471 images, each trained under one schedule and scored by surface distances at native resolution. FETALFusion reaches a Dice score of 0.963 and an HD95 of 2.10 mm without test-time augmentation or a domain label. It improves on U-Mamba on all five reported metrics (HD95 reduced by 0.31 mm; Holm-corrected ($p < 10^{-4}$), a lead that holds under test-time augmentation and across two independent training runs, and in the mean on U-Net, Attention U-Net and TransUNet. Residual encoders close the gap: a ResNet-34 UNet++ exceeds FETALFusion, and an ImageNet initialised ResNet-34 U-Net is best overall (HD95 1.75 mm). The ablation agrees. Calibrated against run-to-run variation, it attributes FETALFusion's measurable gains to the landmark shape prior and, on transperineal images, to the domain gates, while removing the state-space branch does not measurably change accuracy. HC from the predicted masks agrees with the clinical reference at an intraclass correlation of 0.9986.

title: dMRI-F: A Foundation Model for Generalizable Diffusion MRI Analysis from Sparse Acquisitions
abstract: Diffusion MRI (dMRI) probes water diffusion within the brain, providing unique information about tissue microstructure and white matter connectivity. High-quality dMRI enables advanced and accurate analyses but demands dense acquisitions, resulting in long scan times and hardware constraints that are often infeasible. Further, dMRI requires dedicated computational methods to support diverse analysis tasks (e.g., parcellation, registration, and synthesis) for both neuroscientific and clinical applications. Here, we present dMRI-F, a foundation model that unifies dMRI data enhancement and downstream tasks across diverse acquisitions and populations, while requiring only minimal acquisition input. dMRI-F is pre-trained with a q-space masked reconstruction task: predicting densely sampled multi-shell data from only six volumes. It learns generalizable latent feature representations of dMRI data, which serve as a core foundation for adapting to diverse downstream tasks, including brain parcellation, brain registration, and cross-modal synthesis. Across nine independently acquired datasets, we demonstrate that dMRI-F outperforms state-of-the-art methods with robust generalization across acquisitions, populations, and tasks. Our results demonstrate dMRI-F's versatility as a general-purpose framework that enables diverse dMRI applications from low-cost, sparse acquisitions.

title: SYNPRED: A Synergistic Approach to Multimodal Learning for Clinical Prediction
abstract: Multimodal medical data captures complementary aspects of disease. It provides a comprehensive basis for diagnosis and the identification of biological associations linked to progression or treatment response. Established contrastive learning approaches exploit shared information across modalities, but fall short in exploiting complementary, modality-specific signals relevant for a task. Here, we propose a synergistic multimodal variational autoencoder (VAE) framework that separates task-relevant unimodal and multimodal information from instance-specific variation task-irrelevant, allowing complementary signals across modalities to be leveraged for prediction. The method yields benefits even if modalities are missing at test time. We evaluate the method on a treatment response prediction task using medical imaging and RNA data. Empirical comparison with alignment-based and multimodal VAE state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates improved multimodal prediction performance, and consistent benefits for prediction from a single modality after multimodal training. The full code can be found here: https://github.com/cirmuw/SYNPRED.

title: Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration for Dual-Student Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Dual-student learning enriches predictive diversity in SSMIS by introducing a strongly augmented view alongside a weakly augmented view. Insufficient strong augmentation may homogenize the students, whereas excessive augmentation can corrupt anatomical evidence and destabilize collaboration. This challenge echoes feedback-regulated human instruction, where learners receive differentiated tasks and the task difficulty is continually adjusted according to their evolving responses. Inspired by these, we propose Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration (HAC), a closed-loop dual-student framework that maintains weak--strong learning through adaptive difficulty calibration and geometry preservation. Specifically, Reinforcement-guided Difficulty Calibration (RDC) formulates strong-augmentation control as a window-level reinforcement learning process, using augmentation history, realized perturbations, and training responses to dynamically adjust the augmentation magnitude, operation number, and magnitude range. Meanwhile, the Gramian Geometry Preservation Constraint (G2PC) preserves the early-stage three-branch geometry through global volume and pairwise area constraints, preventing shared supervision from homogenizing the two students. Comprehensive evaluations across LA, Pancreas, and BraTS-2019 validate both the segmentation effectiveness and capability-aware difficulty calibration of HAC.

title: LiFUSE: Frequency-Spatial Unified Self-Supervised Pretraining for Liver Disease Analysis on Non-contrast CT
abstract: Given the growing global burden of liver tumors and diffuse liver diseases, non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) is increasingly used for opportunistic screening because of its low cost and favorable safety profile. However, downstream tasks such as tumor detection and fine-grained disease diagnosis remain challenging due to NCCT's inherently low tissue contrast, lack of hemodynamic enhancement, and complex anatomical background. These limitations make subtle, heterogeneous, and multifocal hepatic lesions difficult to identify. Although large-scale self-supervised pretraining can learn robust representations from unlabeled NCCT scans, conventional voxel-wise reconstruction does not fully exploit the complementary information available in NCCT. Under weak NCCT contrast, low-level intensity patterns become less informative for pathology recognition, limiting the capture of lesion-specific discriminative features. In this paper, we propose the Liver Frequency-Spatial Unified Self-Supervised Pretraining (LiFUSE). The frequency branch applies random band-stop masking and spectrum reconstruction to encourage the model to capture subtle differences between lesions and surrounding tissues, while the spatial branch performs hybrid-granularity masked volumetric reconstruction to accommodate lesions of diverse sizes and morphologies. Finally, a cross-domain consistency scheme couples the spatial and frequency branches, yielding more discriminative representations for hepatic structures and lesions. Extensive experiments on three clinically relevant tasks across internal cohorts and a public target-domain transfer setting show that LiFUSE consistently outperforms strong baselines. These results suggest that unified frequency-spatial learning can improve liver disease analysis on NCCT, highlighting its potential for large-scale screening.

title: Noise2Match: Self-Supervised Low-Dose CT Denoising via Adaptive Inter-Slice Matching
abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning, supervised convolutional neural network methods have greatly improved the performance of low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising. However, they require paired noisy-clean training data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. Some classic self-supervised denoising methods rely on the assumption of pixel-wise independent noise, making them ineffective for correlated noise in low-dose CT (LDCT) images. Considering the high similarity and weaker noise correlation between adjacent CT slices, several recently proposed self-supervised methods use adjacent LDCT slices for training. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to effectively account for the non-rigid misalignment between slices caused by anatomical variation, hindering them from satisfying the equal-mean condition required by the classic Noise2Noise framework. In this paper, we propose Noise2Match, a self-supervised LDCT denoising method based on adaptive inter-slice matching. Noise2Match introduces an inter-slice matching network to model the label transition process between adjacent slices, and then applies correction to the denoiser's outputs to better satisfy the equal-mean condition. We theoretically prove that, under idealized conditions, training Noise2Match using adjacent LDCT slices is equivalent to supervised training with paired noisy-clean images. We further find that Noise2Match can also effectively perform low-dose conebeam CT (CBCT) denoising, which could be attributed to its correction operation that reduces inter-slice noise correlation. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Match is the first effective image-domain self-supervised method for low-dose CBCT. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Noise2Match outperforms existing image-domain selfsupervised methods, offering broader applicability and higher practical value.
