title: Development and External Testing of an Interpretable MRI-Based Machine Learning Model for Differentiating Endometrial Stromal Sarcoma from Cellular Leiomyoma.
abstract: This retrospective two-center diagnostic study was aimed at developing and externally testing an interpretable MRI-based machine learning model for differentiating endometrial stromal sarcoma (ESS) from cellular leiomyoma (CL). A total of 155 women with pathologically confirmed ESS or CL were assigned to a derivation cohort (n = 111) and an external testing cohort (n = 44). Clinical variables, qualitative MRI features, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) histogram parameters were evaluated. Three MRI-derived predictors-irregular tumor margin, cystic areas on T2-weighted imaging, and mean ADC-were used to train six classifiers. The final support vector machine model with a radial basis function kernel was evaluated at a fixed threshold determined in the derivation cohort using receiver operating characteristic, calibration, decision curve, and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analyses. A reader study assessed the effect of model assistance. The model achieved areas under the curve of 0.843 (95% CI, 0.760-0.917) in the derivation cohort and 0.835 (95% CI, 0.669-0.960) in the external testing cohort. Calibration and decision curve analyses indicated acceptable performance and potential clinical utility. In an exploratory model-assisted reader analysis, junior radiologist specificity increased from 46.4 to 82.1% and accuracy from 52.3 to 77.3%. This interpretable three-feature model demonstrated promising performance across cohorts and may serve as an adjunctive tool for preoperative MRI assessment, although prospective multicenter validation is warranted.

The final support vector machine model with a radial basis function kernel was evaluated at a fixed threshold determined in the derivation cohort using receiver operating characteristic, calibration, decision curve, and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analyses. A reader study assessed the effect of model assistance. The model achieved areas under the curve of 0.843 (95% CI, 0.760-0.917) in the derivation cohort and 0.835 (95% CI, 0.669-0.960) in the external testing cohort. Calibration and decision curve analyses indicated acceptable performance and potential clinical utility. In an exploratory model-assisted reader analysis, junior radiologist specificity increased from 46.4 to 82.1% and accuracy from 52.3 to 77.3%. This interpretable three-feature model demonstrated promising performance across cohorts and may serve as an adjunctive tool for preoperative MRI assessment, although prospective multicenter validation is warranted.

title: Generalizability of Deep Learning Architectures for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma Classification in Histopathology: A Comparative CNN-Vision Transformer Study with External Validation and Label-Quality Analysis.
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the most prevalent oral malignancy, with delayed diagnosis contributing to poor survival. Deep learning has shown promise for histopathological detection of OSCC, but reported performance is frequently based on single-source datasets, with limited external validation and variable annotation quality. Our study was to compare representative CNN and transformer architectures for histopathological OSCC classification and assess their generalizability under external domain shift. A total of 10,817 H&E-stained image patches from 114 patients were classified as OSCC or normal/control. Images were independently reviewed by two oral pathologists, with discordant cases adjudicated by a senior pathologist (Cohen's κ = 0.975). Eight ImageNet-pre-trained architectures (ResNet18, ResNet50, ResNet101, DenseNet121, EfficientNet-B0, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ViT-B/16, and Swin-T) were fine-tuned using three random seeds. Models were trained, validated, and tested on the internally curated dataset {MIDAS} and subsequently evaluated on two independent external datasets used exclusively for external validation. Diagnostic performance, computational efficiency, statistical significance, and model interpretability were assessed. To investigate the observed reduction in external performance, cancer-labelled images from the external datasets underwent post hoc expert pathological review for potential label discordance. A total of 10,817 H&E-stained image patches from 114 patients were classified as OSCC or normal/control. Images were independently reviewed by two oral pathologists, with discordant cases adjudicated by a senior pathologist (Cohen's κ = 0.975). Eight ImageNet-pre-trained architectures (ResNet18, ResNet50, ResNet101, DenseNet121, EfficientNet-B0, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ViT-B/16, and Swin-T) were fine-tuned using three random seeds. Models were evaluated on a patient-level internal test set and two independent external datasets. Diagnostic performance, computational efficiency, statistical differences, and interpretability were assessed. Cancer-labelled images from External Dataset 2 were post hoc reassessed for label discordance. ConvNeXt-Tiny demonstrated the strongest overall performance. Substantial external degradation across models highlights the effects of domain shift and label quality, emphasizing expert annotation, independent validation, reproducible benchmarking, and multi-institutional datasets for clinical translation.

title: Interpretable Source-Aware Bone-Muscle Fusion Framework for Multicenter Prediction of Osteoporotic Vertebral Fractures.
abstract: Osteoporotic vertebral fracture (OVF) is underrecognized, and bone mineral density (BMD) alone may be insufficient for prediction. We developed the multisource fusion model for osteoporotic vertebral fracture (MSF-OVF), an interpretable source-aware framework integrating clinical-demographic variables, BMD, and lumbar MRI-derived ventral and dorsal paraspinal muscle (PM) representations. This retrospective multicenter study included 2680 participants aged > 40 years from five centers (one training, one internal validation, four external test cohorts). Deep features from four PM regions were extracted using vision foundation model-guided transfer learning and integrated with age, sex, body mass index, and BMD through source-aware latent fusion. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), calibration, and interpretability analyses. MSF-OVF achieved an AUC of 0.881 (95% CI, 0.854-0.909) in internal validation and 0.851-0.917 across four external cohorts. Compared with the clinical-demographic and BMD baseline, MSF-OVF improved AUC by 0.046-0.093 and significantly outperformed it in internal validation and most external cohorts (DeLong P ≤ 0.034). Continuous NRI was 0.268-1.034 across all validation cohorts (P ≤ 0.011). MSF-OVF also outperformed single-muscle models (AUC, 0.454-0.736; P ≤ 0.009). After training-derived logistic recalibration, the internal validation Brier score was 0.140, with a calibration-in-the-large (CITL) of - 0.168 and calibration slope of 0.926. Class activation maps mainly highlighted PM regions. Automated segmentation took several seconds and inference 57.71 ± 18.66 ms per participant. Source-aware fusion of clinical-demographic, BMD, and PM MRI information may support computer-aided multicenter OVF prediction.

title: Deep Learning-Based Automated Computed Tomography Classification of Posterior Malleolar Fractures for a Standardized Diagnostic Framework.
abstract: Despite advances in computed tomography (CT)-based classification systems for posterior malleolar fractures (PMFs), diagnostic consistency remains limited because these systems are still highly dependent on the observer's experience. This study aimed to develop a deep learning-based automated model capable of classifying PMFs according to the Haraguchi, Mason-Molloy, and Bartoníček-Rammelt clasification systems using CT scans, and to compare the classification performance of different convolutional neural network architectures. Retrospectively collected preoperative CT data from 480 adult patients with PMFs were analyzed. A total of 2398 CT slices were independently classified by three orthopedic surgeons according to the three classification systems, and majority consensus was used as the reference standard. Anonymized DICOM images were evaluated using VGG-16, ResNet-101, and DenseNet-121 architectures. The dataset was divided into 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% testing subsets. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, precision, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). The VGG-16 and ResNet-101 models demonstrated high classification performance in the Haraguchi and Mason-Molloy systems. In the VGG-16 model, AUC values exceeded 0.90 across most fracture subtypes, reaching particularly high levels in Haraguchi types I-III, Mason-Molloy types IIB and III, and Bartoníček-Rammelt type IV. Similarly, the ResNet-101 model achieved AUC values above 0.90 in most classes, with very high discriminative performance observed in selected subtypes. F1-scores were greater than 0.70 among most fracture categories and exceeded 0.80 in several, indicating strong and consistent classification performance. These findings demonstrate that deep learning-based automated CT classification of PMFs is feasible and diagnostically robust. The proposed framework may improve diagnostic consistency, reduce observer-dependent variability, and support standardized assessment of posterior malleolar fractures in clinical practice.

title: Explainability and Clinical Trust of Deep Learning in Glioblastoma Treatment Efficacy Prediction: A Comprehensive Framework.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) treatment response is highly heterogeneous. Predicting outcomes from pre-treatment MRI is a critical unmet need, yet the clinical adoption of "black box" deep learning (DL) models is hindered by a lack of transparency. Robust and holistic validation frameworks still need to be developed to allow clinical trust. A multi-layered eXplainable AI (XAI) pipeline was employed to dissect a previously developed deep learning model trained to predict GBM overall survival. First, the model's visual focus was qualitatively and quantitatively analysed. Second, the model's feature dependence was quantified using input ablation studies. Third, the depth at which class information becomes decodable was traced by linear probing of the internal representations. Finally, the clinical impact of the AI and its explanations was assessed in a multi-reader, multi-case study (37 patients, 4 readers, 3 phases, 444 observations) using Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) and clustered bootstrapping. Analysis revealed a high-intensity heuristic: hyper-intense pixels at the skull periphery anchored "Long-Term" predictions, while the model defaulted to "Short-Term" based on tumour enhancement in its absence. The ablation study established this dependence, and linear probing pointed in the same direction. In the clinical study, AI assistance significantly improved expert accuracy (OR 1.598, p < 0.01) without artificially boosting confidence (p = 0.561). Importantly, the addition of XAI heatmaps was associated with a change in how experts used the AI score (interaction p < 0.01), and with fewer patients wrongly called long-term survivors. High predictive accuracy can mask reliance on low-level intensity heuristics. While superficial interpretation of saliency maps is perilous, multi-layered audits expose these shortcuts. Clinically, spatial heatmaps were associated with improved expert diagnostic accuracy and a shift in decision-making strategy.

Importantly, the addition of XAI heatmaps was associated with a change in how experts used the AI score (interaction p < 0.01), and with fewer patients wrongly called long-term survivors. High predictive accuracy can mask reliance on low-level intensity heuristics. While superficial interpretation of saliency maps is perilous, multi-layered audits expose these shortcuts. Clinically, spatial heatmaps were associated with improved expert diagnostic accuracy and a shift in decision-making strategy.

title: From Intra- to Inter-habitat Analysis: Spatial Structure Features for Axillary Lymph Node Metastasis Prediction on Breast DCE-MRI.
abstract: Habitat radiomics characterizes texture within tumor subregions but discards the spatial relationships between them. We developed a landscape-ecology-inspired framework quantifying inter-habitat spatial structure on DCE-MRI, evaluated its complementary value alongside within-habitat radiomics, and compared early versus late fusion, using axillary lymph node metastasis (ALNM) prediction as the evaluation task. In this multicenter retrospective study, 284 patients from one center were randomly split into training (n = 198) and validation (n = 86) cohorts, with 120 patients from an independent institution as the external test set. Tumors were partitioned into six habitats by k-means clustering of 19 voxel-wise texture descriptors, with centroids derived exclusively from the training cohort. Three feature domains were constructed: 8 clinical parameters, 642 within-habitat radiomics features, and 94 inter-habitat spatial structure features spanning fragmentation (n = 30), morphology (n = 24), inter-habitat contact (n = 15), inter-habitat distance (n = 15), area ratio (n = 6), and diversity (n = 4). In the external test set, progressive fusion yielded incremental gains in AUC: clinical alone 0.754, plus within-habitat radiomics 0.843, plus inter-habitat spatial structure 0.863 (95% CI 0.792-0.934). The full early fusion model achieved higher AUC than the clinical-only (DeLong P = 0.011) and spatial-structure-only models (P = 0.044); early fusion yielded a numerically higher AUC than late fusion without reaching significance (0.863 vs 0.851, P = 0.636). The two single-domain imaging models were statistically indistinguishable (0.817 vs 0.784, P = 0.512). Inter-habitat spatial structure captures tumor organization overlooked by conventional habitat radiomics and provides complementary information for preoperative ALNM prediction.

title: Semi-Automated Image Labeling and Object Tracking for MR-Guided Radiotherapy Using a Foundation Vision Model.
abstract: Magnetic resonance-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) enables real-time tracking of tumor and organ motion for more precise radiation delivery. However, existing clinical tracking software struggles with high-velocity or non-rigid motion. Foundation models, such as Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) and MedSAM2, offer robust tracking with fast inference speeds and strong zero-shot accuracy that can improve with fine-tuning. Fine-tuning typically uses expert-labeled datasets, which are expensive to acquire. We explored SAM2's utility in accelerating the labeling process by developing a workflow where novices label < 1% of frames and SAM2 automatically labels the rest. We then evaluated SAM2 and MedSAM2 for tumor tracking on an open-access MRgRT dataset in three configurations: zero-shot, fine-tuned using manually labeled data, and fine-tuned using the semi-automatically labeled data. We measured accuracy with the Dice similarity coefficient, 95th percentile (P95) Hausdorff distance, and centroid distance. MedSAM2 and SAM2 demonstrated strong zero-shot tracking accuracy with no significant difference among the model variants. Fine-tuning significantly improved Dice coefficients (0.874 to 0.891, p = 0.006), P95 Hausdorff distances (9.069 to 4.378 mm, p < 0.001), and centroid distances (5.299 to 1.769 mm, p < 0.001) relative to zero-shot, with no significant difference between using manually labeled and semi-automatically labeled data. Therefore, leveraging SAM2 to semi-automatically generate labeled training data can substantially reduce the cost of data curation and long-term model maintenance without compromising accuracy.

title: CSNet: Cognitive Simulation Network for Reliable Histopathology-Based Cancer Diagnosis.
abstract: Histopathology-based cancer diagnosis is crucial for early detection and timely therapeutic intervention. However, most deep learning methods for histopathological image classification are mainly optimized as prediction models, with limited consideration of clinical diagnostic workflows. In routine practice, pathologists usually follow a sequential reasoning process: coarse assessment of possible abnormalities, detailed inspection of suspicious regions, and consultation-based reasoning to reduce uncertainty. To provide more reliable and interpretable decision support for histopathology-based cancer diagnosis, we propose the cognitive simulation network (CSNet), which draws inspiration from pathologists' sequential diagnostic workflow. First, the multi-view fuzzy assessment module integrates frequency, texture, and gradient cues through learnable fuzzy membership functions to estimate view-level abnormality degrees, providing an initial assessment of suspicious pathological evidence. Guided by this assessment, the gradient-guided fuzzy modulator converts abnormality information into spatial guidance, enhancing informative high-gradient morphological responses while suppressing redundant low-informative regions. Based on the modulated representations, the uncertainty-guided multi-expert synergy mechanism estimates diagnostic uncertainty and coordinates multiple expert branches to generate consensus representations for reliable prediction. Extensive experiments on Kather-5 K, LC25000, LC25000-clean, and a collected cervical cancer histopathology dataset demonstrate that CSNet achieves superior performance, with accuracies of 97.673%, 99.964%, 97.920%, and 99.861%, respectively. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the proposed designs, and statistical analyses confirm the reliability of the observed improvements. Meanwhile, robustness evaluations and comparative visualizations demonstrate stable performance and more consistent responses in diagnostically relevant tissue regions, highlighting the potential of CSNet for reliable histopathology-based cancer diagnosis.

title: Comparison of the Performances of Deep Learning Methods in Kellgren-Lawrence Classification of Knee Osteoarthritis: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) causes symptoms such as pain, stiffness, and functional limitation in the knees; plain knee radiographs are used in addition to physical examination in its diagnosis. This study aimed to compare the performance of pre-trained deep learning models in knee OA classification and to examine the effects of lateral knee radiographs and patient clinical data on the performance of these models. Eight centers participated in the study; radiographs from six centers were used for training, validation, and testing of the models, and radiographs from two centers were used for external validation. In addition to anteroposterior (AP) and lateral knee radiographs, clinical information such as age, gender, height, and weight was collected from the patients. A total of 1550 patients were included in the study. The performance of deep learning models VGG-16, ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, Inception_v3, and EfficientNetb0 was compared in the classification of knee OA. The VGG-16 model yielded significantly higher performance metrics than competing architectures (p < 0.001), with an accuracy of 0.73, sensitivity of 0.72, specificity of 0.93, F1 score of 0.72, positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.72, quadratic weighted Kappa of 0.91, and AUC of 0.93. Feature extraction was performed using the VGG-16 model, and the patient's age, gender, and BMI clinical characteristics were added to the image feature set and classified using machine learning algorithms. The XGBoost classifier showed statistically insignificant improvements of 1-2% in performance metrics. Similar performance results were obtained with the VGG-16 model in a study using only AP knee radiographs. Radiographs from two centers were used for external validation, and the VGG-16 model yielded accuracy of 0.65, sensitivity of 0.65, specificity of 0.91, PPV of 0.67, F1 score of 0.65, quadratic weighted kappa of 0.88, and AUC of 0.90. Adding age, gender, and BMI clinical characteristics to the knee radiograph image feature set did not significantly improve model performance. Furthermore, adding lateral radiographs to the AP knee radiograph set did not provide any additional contribution to KL classification performance.

title: AI-based Hip Fracture Classification from Pelvic X-ray Images Using a Hybrid PEFT-ViT and XGBoost Model.
abstract: Accurate radiographic classification of hip fractures into femoral neck (intracapsular) versus intertrochanteric (extracapsular) types is essential for surgical planning, yet most AI studies focus on binary detection using large datasets from high-resource regions, with no prior work from the Middle East. This study proposes a Hybrid PEFT-ViT and XGBoost framework for three-class classification of hip radiographs (Normal, Intertrochanteric fracture, Neck of femur fracture), using 768 X-ray images collected from King Abdullah University Hospital (KAUH) in Northern Jordan. A LoRA-fine-tuned ViT-Base/16 backbone extracted fused class-token and patch-token features, which were classified using XGBoost. On an independent test set of 77 radiographs, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 88.31% (95% CI 79.3-93.7%), a sensitivity of 87.75%, a specificity of 94.28%, and an F1-score of 87.75%, the highest among the evaluated CNN-based (MobileNetV2, DenseNet121) and transformer-based (ViT, DeiT, Swin) baselines. These results show that clinically meaningful hip fracture classification can be achieved using a single-center dataset, providing a practical framework for resource-limited settings, although external validation is still required.

title: Validation of a Deep Learning Model for Automated Ureteral Length Measurement on CT Against Gross Specimens.
abstract: This study validates a deep learning model for automated ureteral length measurement on CT using gross specimen measurements as the reference standard. A deep learning model was trained on 3629 CT series from 1502 patients (cohort 1) to segment the ureter and extract centerline length. An independent prospective cohort (cohort 2) of 70 patients undergoing radical nephroureterectomy served as the hold-out test set. Each gross specimen was measured twice by one urologist (D1_length and D2_length), with their mean as the reference length (Ref_length). Model-predicted lengths (AI_length) were compared with Ref_length using repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests. Determinants of discrepancy were assessed with Spearman correlation and multiple linear regression. Marginal means (± SE) were 266 ± 3.85 mm (D1_length), 273 ± 3.25 mm (D2_length), 269 ± 2.75 mm (AI_length), and 269 ± 3.45 mm (Ref_length). Measurement method had a statistically significant but negligible effect on length (F(3, 207) = 2.73, p = 0.045, η 2 G = 0.007). D1_length and D2_length differed significantly from Ref_length (both p = 0.002), whereas AI_length was not statistically different from Ref_length (p > 0.999). In regression analysis, reference ureteral length was the only independently associated variable (coefficient - 0.54 mm per mm of reference length, 95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.39; p < 0.001); age, sex, body height, body weight, operation side, and lesion location were not significantly associated. The proposed deep learning pipeline achieved accurate fully automated ureteral segmentation and length measurement across diverse CT acquisition phases and demonstrated close agreement with surgical gross specimen measurements in a prospective clinical cohort, supporting its potential to assist preoperative planning and reduce reliance on manual measurement. The measurement discrepancy was governed primarily by ureteral length itself-with a small systematic underestimation in longer ureters-rather than by patient or procedural factors. However, this tendency, together with the single-center design, and the modest size of the prospective cohort, warrants further multicenter validation before routine clinical deployment.

title: Use of Machine Learning and Imaging to Predict Outcomes After Lumbar Spine Surgery: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Postoperative outcomes following lumbar spine surgery remain variable, and existing clinical risk stratification methods offer limited predictive accuracy. Advances in machine learning enable quantitative analysis of routinely acquired spinal imaging, creating opportunities to improve preoperative outcome prediction. However, the methodological quality and clinical readiness of imaging-based machine learning models in lumbar spine surgery have not been systematically evaluated. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched through October 2025 for studies using machine learning models trained on imaging data (MRI, CT, or radiographs) to predict postoperative outcomes after lumbar spine surgery. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST). Twenty-six studies published between 2019 and 2025 met inclusion criteria. Most models predicted patient-reported or clinical outcomes, with fewer addressing complications, structural outcomes, or imaging-derived biomarkers. MRI was the predominant modality. Model discrimination was frequently moderate to high (median AUC, 0.83), though external validation and calibration reporting were uncommon. All studies demonstrated high risk of bias, primarily related to analysis and validation practices. Imaging-based machine learning models show promise for improving preoperative outcome prediction after lumbar spine surgery, but methodological limitations limit current clinical applicability. Greater emphasis on external validation, standardized outcomes, and prospective evaluation is needed to support safe translation into routine spine care.

title: Impact of different pre-processing methods combined with combat harmonization on the reproducibility of radiomics features in healthy human brain MRI.
abstract: Objective To explore the effect of different pre-processing methods combined with ComBat harmonization on improving the stability of MRI radiomic features in healthy human brains. Methods T1FLAIR and T2W scans from 416 healthy subjects across four MRI systems underwent seven pipelines (Original, N4, Z-Score, DTN, Nyul, WhiteStripe, RAVEL). SynthSeg segmented white/gray matter for 93 IBSI radiomic features. Stability was quantified via covariate-adjusted standardized scanner effect (d = β_scanner/σ_res, |d|< 0.2) with 95% bootstrap CIs, supplemented by PCA and LOOCV AUC. Friedman and post-hoc McNemar tests with Bonferroni correction compared pipelines. FDR-corrected partial correlations assessed retention of significant age and sex associations after ComBat. Results Raw data exhibited extremely low stability with substantial scanner-induced effects, while scanner classification AUC was close to 1.0. ComBat harmonization significantly improved stability across all pipelines and reduced AUC to near 0.5. Within this dataset, DTN_ComBat demonstrated consistently high stability; pairwise statistical comparisons indicated it showed more favourable stability performance relative to most other pipelines for the majority of tested contrasts, with stable proportions exceeding 90% across all sequences and tissues, and retained 75.0-100.0% of statistically significant age and sex-related associations. Conclusion Unprocessed brain MRI radiomic features exhibit poor cross‑scanner stability. Within this dataset, ComBat effectively reduces scanner‑related feature‑distribution differences, while preserving most statistically‑significant age and sex‑related associations. Among tested pre-processing pipelines, DTN_ComBat showed comparatively favourable performance under the present healthy‑brain MRI scanner‑protocol configurations.
originalAbstract:
Objective

To explore the effect of different pre-processing methods combined with ComBat harmonization on improving the stability of MRI radiomic features in healthy human brains.

Methods

T1FLAIR and T2W scans from 416 healthy subjects across four MRI systems underwent seven pipelines (Original, N4, Z-Score, DTN, Nyul, WhiteStripe, RAVEL). SynthSeg segmented white/gray matter for 93 IBSI radiomic features. Stability was quantified via covariate-adjusted standardized scanner effect (d = β_scanner/σ_res, |d|< 0.2) with 95% bootstrap CIs, supplemented by PCA and LOOCV AUC. Friedman and post-hoc McNemar tests with Bonferroni correction compared pipelines. FDR-corrected partial correlations assessed retention of significant age and sex associations after ComBat.

Results

Raw data exhibited extremely low stability with substantial scanner-induced effects, while scanner classification AUC was close to 1.0. ComBat harmonization significantly improved stability across all pipelines and reduced AUC to near 0.5. Within this dataset, DTN_ComBat demonstrated consistently high stability; pairwise statistical comparisons indicated it showed more favourable stability performance relative to most other pipelines for the majority of tested contrasts, with stable proportions exceeding 90% across all sequences and tissues, and retained 75.0-100.0% of statistically significant age and sex-related associations.

Conclusion

Unprocessed brain MRI radiomic features exhibit poor cross‑scanner stability. Within this dataset, ComBat effectively reduces scanner‑related feature‑distribution differences, while preserving most statistically‑significant age and sex‑related associations. Among tested pre-processing pipelines, DTN_ComBat showed comparatively favourable performance under the present healthy‑brain MRI scanner‑protocol configurations.

title: Radiological features of peritumoral brain injury and neurological outcomes after glioma surgery: a prospective observational study.
abstract: Purpose Despite significant advances in glioma surgery, early postoperative neuroimaging frequently reveals signs of surgical brain injury (SBI). This prospective observational study aimed to investigate the incidence, radiological characteristics, neurological outcomes and risk factors of SBI following glioma resection. Methods Patients with newly diagnosed supratentorial gliomas who undergo tumor resection were prospectively enrolled. Serial MRI examinations were administrated early postoperative (≤ 72 h) and on postoperative days 7, 14 and 28 to assess the characteristics of infarction, edema and microhemorrhage. Neurological outcomes were evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at postoperative day 28. Results A total of 64 patients was included. Postoperative infarction was identified in 14 patients (21.9%), with all anatomically localized to the basal ganglia, thalamus, or insular regions. Intraoperative blood loss ≥ 300 mL was independently associated with postoperative infarction (Odd Ratio [OR]: 4.62, p = 0.035). Microhemorrhage was observed in 53.8% of patients. Peritumoral edema occurred in all cases and exhibited two distinct patterns: residual tumor-associated edema (n = 42) and de novo surgery-induced edema (n = 22). The average volume of tumor-associated edema decreased, whereas that of surgery-induced edema increased over time. Among the 53 patients who completed neurological outcome assessments, 13 developed disability (mRS ≥ 2). Risk factors were higher intraoperative blood loss (OR: 8.88, p = 0.013) and postoperative infarction (OR: 6.33, p = 0.031). Conclusion SBI, including infarction and edema, is common following glioma surgery and associated with adverse neurological outcomes. Meticulous intraoperative hemostatic management is essential to prevent postoperative infarction and even disability outcome.

title: Limited clinical value of routine PET/CT in early-stage breast cancer: a multicenter retrospective study.
abstract: Background Staging of breast cancer at diagnosis is essential for prognosis and guiding treatment decisions. The role of ^18F-FDG positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) in patients with asymptomatic early-stage breast cancer remains controversial because of the low prevalence of distant metastasis and risk of false-positive findings. Materials and methods This is a retrospective multicenter cohort study across three tertiary centers in Lebanon. Adult patients with newly diagnosed stage I or IIA breast cancer who underwent PET/CT for initial staging between January 2019 and December 2024 were included. Patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy prior to imaging or with more advanced disease were excluded. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize outcomes, including rates of disease upstaging and false-positive findings. Results A total of 435 patients were included. Most tumors were invasive ductal carcinoma (88.0%) and hormone receptor-positive (ER 88.5%, PR 81.4%), with HER2 positivity in 17.7%. PET/CT resulted in stage upstaging in 23 patients (5.3%), 12 patients upstaged to stage IIA, 5 to stage IIB, and 6 to stage IV. However, histopathology confirmed distant metastases in only 3 patients (0.7%, 3/435). Overall, upstaging was pathologically confirmed in 11 patients, whereas it was not confirmed in 12 patients, with the discordant cases being predominantly attributable to false-positive nodal findings. PET/CT findings led to treatment modification in only 0.9% (4/435) of the cohort. Conclusion In this cohort of asymptomatic patients with clinical stage I-IIA breast cancer, PET/CT rarely identifies additional metastatic disease and frequently results in false-positive findings. These results suggest a selective, risk-adapted use of PET/CT rather than routine staging in early-stage breast cancer, particularly in resource-constrained healthcare settings, and should be interpreted in the context of the study's retrospective design.

title: Wireless versus cart-based ultrasound in musculoskeletal and superficial soft-tissue imaging: a prospective blinded cross-over study.
abstract: Aim Wireless ultrasound probes are increasingly used in point-of-care settings, but their performance in musculoskeletal and superficial soft-tissue imaging remains incompletely defined. This study compared image quality and clinical-pragmatic performance of a wireless ultrasound probe with a high-end cart-based ultrasound system. Methods This prospective blinded cross-over study included 41 musculoskeletal or superficial soft-tissue anatomical regions examined in routine clinical practice. Each region was assessed with both the Mindray Resona I9 Elite Edition cart-based system and the Mindray TE-Air e5M wireless probe. Device order was randomized. Images were acquired by one experienced operator, anonymized, coded, and reviewed offline by an experienced reviewer blinded to device type. Image quality, anatomical margin definition, tissue contrast, speckle noise, diagnostic confidence, interpretability, diagnosis possibility, pathological finding detection, clinical decision sufficiency, and the need for further imaging were assessed. Results The cart-based system showed superior image quality. Median global image quality was 5 versus 3, anatomical margin definition 5 versus 3 and tissue contrast 5 versus 4. Diagnostic confidence was higher with the cart-based system, 97.95 ± 5.32 versus 69.10 ± 16.05. Clinical-pragmatic endpoints showed a less pronounced reduction: examination interpretability was 97.6% versus 90.2%, diagnosis was considered possible in 73.2% versus 61.0%, and images were sufficient for clinical decision-making in 70.7% versus 58.5%. Conclusions The wireless probe provided lower image quality and confidence but retained clinically useful performance in selected cases. It should be considered complementary rather than a substitute for high-end cart-based ultrasound.

title: Comparison of Integrated Versus Sequential Artificial Intelligence-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis Systems in Breast Ultrasound: A Prospective Pilot Study on Examination Time, Reproducibility, and Diagnostic Performance.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To compare integrated and sequential artificial intelligence-based computer-aided diagnosis (AI-CAD) systems in terms of examination time, reproducibility, and diagnostic performance in breast ultrasound (US). Materials and methods This prospective single-center study included women who underwent breast US at a breast imaging center between February and March 2025. Two real-time AI-CAD systems were evaluated: an integrated system providing simultaneous lesion detection and diagnosis during scanning, and a sequential system in which lesion detection and diagnostic assessment were performed separately. Examination time was assessed in patients who underwent paired breast US examinations with both AI-CAD systems during the same visit, with randomized examination order. Reproducibility was assessed by applying both systems twice to the same breast lesions. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results Examination time analysis included 97 patients and showed longer examination time with sequential AI-CAD than with integrated AI-CAD (P < .001), regardless of examination order. Reproducibility analysis included 145 patients with 215 lesions and showed almost perfect agreement between the first and second acquisitions for both systems (integrated vs. sequential: κ = 0.81 vs. 0.83). For the comparison between the first and second acquisitions, κ values for the integrated versus sequential systems were 0.92 versus 0.76 for malignant lesions, 0.79 versus 0.84 for mass lesions, and 1.00 versus 0.75 for nonmass lesions. However, agreement patterns varied across other scan-plane comparisons. Diagnostic performance analysis included 242 patients. Integrated AI-CAD showed higher sensitivity (integrated vs. sequential: 87.6% vs. 76.9%; P < .001), whereas sequential AI-CAD showed higher specificity (integrated vs. sequential: 74.2% vs. 90.0%; P < .001). AUC did not differ between the two systems. Conclusion Integrated and sequential AI-CAD systems showed complementary strengths in breast US. Integrated AI-CAD favored shorter examination time and higher sensitivity, whereas sequential AI-CAD favored higher specificity, with reproducibility differing according to lesion type.

title: Multicenter Comparative Validation of an nnU-Net-Based Automated CT Radiomics Workflow for Acute Pancreatitis Severity Prediction.
abstract: Rationale and objectives Computed tomography radiomics has shown potential for predicting acute pancreatitis (AP) severity, but conventional workflows depend on labor-intensive expert pancreatic segmentation. This study evaluated a no-new-Net (nnU-Net)-based automated segmentation-radiomics workflow against an expert manual-segmentation workflow, using AP severity classification as the downstream task, and assessed the automated workflow externally. Materials and methods This retrospective multicenter study included patients with AP from Center A (n = 214), Center B (n = 56), and Center C (n = 42). Expert manual pancreatic masks served as reference annotations for nnU-Net training and as the comparator for the radiomics workflow. After selecting the optimal nnU-Net configuration, radiomics features were extracted separately from manual and automated regions of interest, and AP severity classifiers were developed using the same analytical framework. Discrimination between the two workflows was compared in the independent internal test cohort using the area under the curve (AUC) and the paired DeLong test, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) and Bonferroni corrections applied to P values. Results In the internal test cohort, the Light Gradient Boosting Machine classifier achieved AUCs of 0.799 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.683-0.915) and 0.733 (95% CI, 0.593-0.873) with manual and automated segmentations, respectively. The absolute AUC difference was 0.066, and the paired DeLong comparison was not statistically significant after FDR correction (FDR-adjusted p = 0.360; Z = 1.1755, unadjusted p = 0.2398). The automated workflow achieved AUCs of 0.784 (95% CI, 0.653-0.915) in Center B and 0.715 (95% CI, 0.559-0.871) in Center C. The selected 2D nnU-Net achieved a mean Dice coefficient of 0.798 during five-fold cross-validation and 0.726 in the independent internal test cohort. Conclusion The nnU-Net-based automated segmentation-radiomics workflow showed no significant difference in discrimination compared with the expert manual workflow in the internal test cohort. It also maintained moderate discrimination across two external cohorts. These findings support the feasibility of reducing dependence on manual pancreatic segmentation, although the present analysis does not establish formal equivalence or interchangeability.

title: Implementation of a Structured Peer Learning Program and Missed Critical Findings in a Large Integrated Radiology Practice: A Baseline Retrospective Analysis.
abstract: Rationale and objectives The American College of Radiology (ACR) defines peer learning as nonpunitive, education-centered case review, separated from individual performance evaluation. We describe a program designed against ACR criteria in a large integrated practice and report first-cycle metrics, including missed critical findings-a narrow subset of major misses. Materials and methods This retrospective analysis spanned 283 radiologists across more than 100 sites between March 30 and May 14, 2026. Cases entered through voluntary worklist submission, risk-event referral, and departmental escalation, and were adjudicated by a fellowship-trained coordinator. A missed critical finding (MCF) required both a finding on the institutional critical results list (provider notification within 30 minutes) and a 4B classification, with agreement between two independent reviewers. Exact (Poisson) 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Results Of 702 submissions, 489 (69.7%) were Learning Opportunities, 187 (26.6%) Great Calls, and 26 (3.7%) Agrees. Of 283 radiologists, 182 (64.3%) submitted at least one case, and 213 (75.3%) received feedback; two conferences were held. Of 17 candidates, reviewers concurred on 7 at initial review; the 10 discordant were resolved by consensus, none meeting criteria. Across 409,122 interpreted studies, the confirmed MCF rate was 0.017 per 1000 (95% CI 0.007-0.035). Seven radiologists (2.5%) had one event; none had more. No confirmed event had been independently filed as a safety event. Conclusion The MCF rate reflects a narrow, time-critical subset ascertained with unmeasured sensitivity against a diluted denominator. It is a conservative internal baseline, not a measure of diagnostic accuracy or individual performance.

title: [Imaging of pulmonary nodules: A diagnostic approach].
abstract: The detection of pulmonary nodules has increased considerably with the widespread use of chest-computed tomography and the development of low-dose CT lung cancer screening. The pulmonary nodule represents a major diagnostic challenge, requiring rigorous evaluation in order to distinguish benign from malignant lesions while limiting unnecessary invasive investigations. Analysis relies on precise morphological characterization (density, size, margins), assessment of persistence and growth over time, and integration of the clinical context. The Fleischner Society guidelines and the protocols derived from organized screening programs now form the basis of standardized management. This article provides a detailed review of the radiological criteria, decision-making algorithms, and the role of transthoracic needle biopsy in the management of pulmonary nodules.

title: Enhanced two-stage cascaded network for high-precision stopping power ratio and functional image generation from conventional CT.
abstract: Purpose Accurate stopping power ratio (SPR) estimation is essential for proton therapy dose calculation; however, SPR and related functional images-electron density (ED), effective atomic number (Zeff), and iodine concentration (IC)-currently require dual-energy CT (DECT), whose clinical adoption is limited by high cost and restricted availability. To our knowledge, no previous study has synthesized DECT-derived functional images directly from conventional single-energy CT (SECT). This study proposes, for the first time, a deep learning framework that generates SPR, ED, Zeff, and IC maps simultaneously from conventional CT, and investigates whether a physics-informed two-stage cascaded architecture can outperform conventional single-stage networks. Methods Seventy-four head-and-neck cancer patients scanned with a dual-layer DECT scanner were retrospectively analyzed. Integrated detector-layer signals provided SECT-equivalent input images, while DECT-derived maps served as references. Four networks were compared: a single-output UNet (UNet-1), a multi-output UNet (UNet-4), a two-stage cascaded UNet (Cascade-UNet), and the proposed enhanced two-stage cascaded model (Cascade-New), which incorporates an asymmetric encoder-decoder with residual vision modules and Mamba-based dense connectivity, and exploits the physical dependency chain CT → ED/Zeff → SPR through a three-term training loss. Models were evaluated on an independent test set using mean absolute error (MAE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity index measure (SSIM), and Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC), with pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results The proposed Cascade-New model achieved the best overall performance: the lowest SPR MAE (11.65 ± 1.58 in units of SPR × 10 -3 vs. 12.99 ± 1.46 for UNet-4, a 10.3% relative reduction), the highest SSIM (0.9971 ± 0.0016), and the strongest correlation (PCC = 0.9996 ± 0.0002). Improvements over UNet-4 in ED, Zeff, and IC synthesis were all statistically significant (all p = 0.031). Visual and error map analyses confirmed its improved performance, particularly in bone and heterogeneous tissue regions. Purpose

Accurate stopping power ratio (SPR) estimation is essential for proton therapy dose calculation; however, SPR and related functional images-electron density (ED), effective atomic number (Zeff), and iodine concentration (IC)-currently require dual-energy CT (DECT), whose clinical adoption is limited by high cost and restricted availability. To our knowledge, no previous study has synthesized DECT-derived functional images directly from conventional single-energy CT (SECT). This study proposes, for the first time, a deep learning framework that generates SPR, ED, Zeff, and IC maps simultaneously from conventional CT, and investigates whether a physics-informed two-stage cascaded architecture can outperform conventional single-stage networks.

Seventy-four head-and-neck cancer patients scanned with a dual-layer DECT scanner were retrospectively analyzed. Integrated detector-layer signals provided SECT-equivalent input images, while DECT-derived maps served as references. The proposed Cascade-New model achieved the best overall performance: the lowest SPR MAE (11.65 ± 1.58 in units of SPR × 10-3 vs. 12.99 ± 1.46 for UNet-4, a 10.3% relative reduction), the highest SSIM (0.9971 ± 0.0016), and the strongest correlation (PCC = 0.9996 ± 0.0002). Improvements over UNet-4 in ED, Zeff, and IC synthesis were all statistically significant (all p = 0.031). Visual and error map analyses confirmed its improved performance, particularly in bone and heterogeneous tissue regions.

This study provides the first demonstration that SPR and other DECT-derived functional images can be synthesized directly from conventional SECT with high precision. title: Laparoscopic Left Renal Vein Transposition for Nutcracker Syndrome: A Single-Center Case Series.
abstract: Background Nutcracker syndrome is a rare vascular compression disorder caused by entrapment of the left renal vein, most commonly between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. Surgical treatment is reserved for patients with persistent and debilitating symptoms; however, evidence regarding minimally invasive approaches remains limited. This study aimed to evaluate the outcomes of laparoscopic left renal vein transposition in patients with symptomatic nutcracker syndrome. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted of nine consecutive patients who underwent laparoscopic left renal vein transposition for symptomatic nutcracker syndrome between 2019 and 2024 at a single tertiary vascular center. Diagnosis was established using contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrating significant left renal vein compression. Perioperative outcomes, complications, length of hospital stay, and clinical symptom resolution during follow-up were assessed. Results The study group included seven women (77.8%) and two men (22.2%), aged 20-52 years. The most common presenting symptom was left flank or lumbar pain. All procedures were completed laparoscopically without conversion to open surgery. Operative time ranged from 180 to 375 minutes, with a median hospital stay of 4 days. One patient experienced major perioperative bleeding requiring transfusion and pleural drainage (Clavien-Dindo IIIb). Most patients achieved complete or substantial symptom relief during follow-up. One patient developed late anastomotic occlusion with symptom recurrence requiring reoperation and venous bypass reconstruction. Conclusions Laparoscopic left renal vein transposition appears to be a safe and effective treatment option for selected patients with symptomatic nutcracker syndrome. The minimally invasive approach provides favorable clinical outcomes with acceptable perioperative morbidity; however, long-term follow-up remains essential because of the risk of anastomotic occlusion and symptom recurrence. Further multicenter studies with larger patient cohorts are required to better define optimal treatment strategies.

title: Distinctive patterns of right-hemisphere vulnerability in cerebral small vessel disease: a gray matter asymmetry study.
abstract: Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a leading cause of vascular cognitive impairment (VCI), characteristically associated with gray matter (GM) loss. However, it remains unclear whether this GM loss exhibits regional interhemispheric asymmetry and how it relates to cognitive function. In this study, 56 CSVD patients and 56 demographically matched healthy controls were included, and structural MRI as well as cognitive and clinical data were collected. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and the GM Asymmetry Index (GMAI; calculated as (L-R)/(L + R), higher values indicate relatively greater left-sided GM) were performed using a study-specific symmetric template. Perivascular spaces were also estimated with a deep learning framework. Partial correlations were tested against multi-domain cognitive performance. Compared with controls, CSVD patients exhibited extensive GM reduction in the right superior and middle frontal gyri as well as in the left hippocampus and putamen. Regional GMAI analyses further suggested altered hemispheric GM loss, with leftward shifts (higher GMAI) in the middle temporal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, and precuneus, and rightward shifts (lower GMAI) in the inferior temporal and fusiform gyri. Additionally, subcortical nuclei exhibited a corresponding leftward lateralization of perivascular space burden. Association analyses showed that right prefrontal volume was positively related to global cognitive scores, whereas left temporal asymmetry tracked cognitive decline. Of note, this right-dominant pattern in prefrontal-related regions is consistent with our activation likelihood estimation meta-analytic re-synthesis of prior VBM evidence and NeuroSynth mapping. Collectively, these findings suggest a distinct topographical vulnerability of the right hemisphere in CSVD and highlight GMAI as a neuroimaging marker for vascular cognitive decline.

title: Diffusion MRI Assessment of White Matter Microstructure and Free-Water Fraction in Drug-Naïve Children with SeLECTS.
abstract: Background Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (SeLECTS) is a common childhood-onset focal epilepsy syndrome. Although seizures are typically self-limited, some children may show neurodevelopmental or cognitive vulnerability. Diffusion MRI may provide insight into white matter alterations in SeLECTS. Objective To evaluate white matter diffusion differences in newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS using tract-based spatial statistics (TBSS) and white matter free-water fraction (FW-WM), and to explore within-patient associations with selected seizure-related and cognitive variables. Methods Fifty-three newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS and 53 healthy controls with a similar age and sex distribution were prospectively enrolled in this cross-sectional case-control study. Diffusion MRI was acquired at 3.0T, and white matter diffusion differences were assessed using TBSS and FW-WM analyses. Voxelwise between-group differences in fractional anisotropy (FA) were tested with age and sex as covariates and corrected using threshold-free cluster enhancement-based family-wise error correction. FW-WM was compared between groups using age- and sex-adjusted general linear models, with additional adjustment for years of education in a sensitivity analysis. Exploratory within-patient associations between imaging measures and selected clinical or cognitive variables were assessed using partial Spearman correlations with false-discovery-rate correction. Results Children with SeLECTS showed lower FA than healthy controls in multiple TBSS-defined white matter regions after correction for multiple comparisons, mainly involving commissural, projection, and association pathways. No between-group differences in mean, axial, or radial diffusivity survived correction for multiple comparisons. FW-WM was higher in the SeLECTS group after adjustment for age and sex (adjusted mean difference = 0.0085; 95% CI, 0.0023 to 0.0147; P = 0.008), with similar results after additional adjustment for education. In exploratory cluster-level analyses, mean FA in a left-sided cluster involving the posterior internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, and sagittal stratum was inversely associated with disease duration after FDR correction (r = -0.413; P = 0.003; q = 0.010). No imaging-cognition or within-patient FW-WM-FA association survived FDR correction. Conclusions Newly diagnosed, drug-naïve children with SeLECTS showed white matter diffusion differences, including lower FA in distributed TBSS-defined regions and higher FW-WM. These findings support diffusion MRI-based characterization of white matter alterations at diagnosis, before antiseizure treatment. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify their clinical and developmental relevance.

title: 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT in Sepsis.
abstract: 18F-Fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tompgraphy/computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) has emerged as a valuable whole-body metabolic imaging modality in sepsis and related systemic infectious disorders. Exploiting increased glucose metabolism in activated inflammatory cells, it facilitates localization of occult infective foci, detection of septic embolization, and guidance of source control when conventional investigations are inconclusive. Evidence demonstrates high diagnostic yield and meaningful impact on clinical management, particularly in sepsis of unknown origin and high-risk bacteraemia. However, diagnostic accuracy depends on appropriate patient preparation and timing. This review summarizes current evidence, practical challenges, emerging applications, and future research priorities for integrating 18F-FDG PET/CT into sepsis care.

title: Perforated and Complicated Cholecystitis: A Narrative Review of Diagnosis, Management, and Differentiation from Gallbladder Cancer.
abstract: Introduction Perforated cholecystitis is a severe complication of gallbladder inflammation that is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis is often challenging because clinical and radiographic findings overlap with those of uncomplicated cholecystitis and, in some cases, gallbladder malignancy. This review summarizes the current evidence regarding the diagnosis, imaging, management strategies, outcomes, and differentiation of perforated cholecystitis from gallbladder cancer. Methods A comprehensive literature review was conducted using PubMed and Embase from inception to May 2026. Eligible studies included full-text articles, case reports, and original research describing perforated cholecystitis with an emphasis on diagnosis, treatment, outcomes, and gallbladder cancer mimicry. Results Gallbladder perforation results from progressive inflammation, ischemia, and mural necrosis, most commonly involving the fundus of the gallbladder. The Niemeier classification categorizes perforations into acute free perforation (Type I), localized perforation with abscess formation (Type II), and chronic perforation with fistula formation (Type III). Advanced age, male sex, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, delayed presentation, and non-operative management were identified as important risk factors. Computed tomography (CT) was the most sensitive diagnostic modality, demonstrating wall defects, pericholecystic collections, abscesses, bilomas, and extraluminal gallstones. Management includes cholecystectomy, percutaneous cholecystostomy, and interval surgery for selected high-risk patients. Evidence regarding the optimal surgical timing remains inconsistent. Chronic perforation and xanthogranulomatous inflammation may closely mimic gallbladder carcinoma on imaging and intraoperative assessment. Conclusion Perforated cholecystitis is a diagnostically challenging and potentially life-threatening condition. CT imaging is central to diagnosis, while management should be individualized according to the patient status and perforation type. Greater recognition of the features distinguishing perforation from gallbladder malignancy may facilitate earlier diagnosis and improve outcomes. When malignancy is a significant consideration, and the patient's condition permits, consider early referral to an HPB surgeon or multidisciplinary hepatobiliary team to guide further diagnostic evaluation, including tissue acquisition when appropriate, and definitive surgical planning.

title: A Novel TCP and NTCP Modeling Framework Incorporating Inter-Fractional Deviations and Biological Effectiveness for Hyper-fractionated Radiotherapy.
abstract: Purpose High-dose hyper-fractionated radiotherapy has been recently included in NCCN guidelines for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC), which clinical outcomes are dependent on actually delivered biologically effective dose (BED). However, most tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models rely on planed physical dose without considering inter-fractional deviations and BED of fractionization. This study aims to develop TCP and NTCP models for LS-SCLC incorporating CBCT-based inter-fractional anatomies and hyper-fractional radiobiological dose. Methods and materials Inter-fractional dose was accumulated based on deformable image registration between CBCT and planning CT (pCT). Both TCP and NTCP were formulated within a BED-based framework, using dose-volume parameters calculated from planned dose and CBCT-based accumulated dose for comparison. The LQ model with "4R" effects and Gompertzian tumor growth (LQRG) and Lyman-Kutcher-Burman (LKB) models were used for TCP and NTCP modeling. Based on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), negative log-likelihood (NLL), and Akaike information criterion (AIC), model performances were assessed for local progression-free survival (LPFS), radiation pneumonitis and radiation esophagitis. Results Compared with pCT dose, CBCT dose showed superior discrimination of normal tissue toxicity. Purpose

High-dose hyper-fractionated radiotherapy has been recently included in NCCN guidelines for limited-stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC), which clinical outcomes are dependent on actually delivered biologically effective dose (BED). However, most tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) models rely on planed physical dose without considering inter-fractional deviations and BED of fractionization. This study aims to develop TCP and NTCP models for LS-SCLC incorporating CBCT-based inter-fractional anatomies and hyper-fractional radiobiological dose.

Methods and materials

Inter-fractional dose was accumulated based on deformable image registration between CBCT and planning CT (pCT). Both TCP and NTCP were formulated within a BED-based framework, using dose-volume parameters calculated from planned dose and CBCT-based accumulated dose for comparison. The LQ model with "4R" effects and Gompertzian tumor growth (LQRG) and Lyman-Kutcher-Burman (LKB) models were used for TCP and NTCP modeling. Based on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), negative log-likelihood (NLL), and Akaike information criterion (AIC), model performances were assessed for local progression-free survival (LPFS), radiation pneumonitis and radiation esophagitis.

Results

Compared with pCT dose, CBCT dose showed superior discrimination of normal tissue toxicity. For grade ≥2 radiation pneumonitis, the CBCT-based NTCP model achieved significantly higher AUC (0.67 vs. 0.59) and lower NLL (62.39 vs. 66.13) than that of the pCT-based mode. Superiority of CBCT-based NTCP model was also observed for grade ≥3 radiation esophagitis, i.e., AUC (0.62 vs. 0.58) and NLL (55.55 vs. 56.64). Using the observed LPFS as reference, marginally improved TCP modeling was observed using CBCT dose than that of pCT, where the AUC values were 0.80 vs. 0.79 (GTV 45 Gy) and 0.77 vs. 0.75 (GTV 54 Gy).

Conclusions

By incorporating inter-fractional deviation and biological effectiveness, the improved accuracy of TCP and NTCP models provides preliminary evidence supporting the treatment planning and toxicity management for LS-SCLC patients treated with the hyper-fractionated radiotherapy, which needs further clinical validation.

title: Comparing Diagnostic Ability of Two Off-the-Shelf Large Language Models with That of Endodontists for Teeth Requiring Initial Root Canal Treatment: A Multicenter Retrospective Investigation.
abstract: Introduction Despite growing interest in large language models (LLMs) for endodontic diagnosis, prior studies have used simulated cases, examination formats, or small selected series. This multicenter retrospective study compared the diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-5.2 and Gemini 3.0 with that of calibrated endodontists across 645 teeth requiring initial root canal treatment. Methods Cases were evaluated across four endpoints: pulpal diagnosis, periapical diagnosis, treatment planning, and case difficulty. Standardized clinical summaries and radiographs were submitted to endodontists and both LLMs using a fixed single-pass protocol. Exact-match accuracy, Cohen's κ, Gwet's AC1, macro-averaged F1 score, McNemar tests, and generalized estimating equations were used for statistical comparison. Results Endpoint accuracies ranged from 74% to 88%. Macro F1 was highest for periapical diagnosis (ChatGPT-5.2, 0.724; Gemini 3.0, 0.719) and lowest for treatment planning (0.385; 0.550), where both models showed lower observed performance in minority categories, interpreted as suggestive given small subgroup sizes. Composite accuracy across the three clinical endpoints was 61.1% (95% CI, 57.4%-64.8%) and 59.4% (95% CI, 55.3%-63.3%), and four-endpoint accuracy was 47.3% (95% CI, 43.3%-51.2%) and 46.2% (95% CI, 42.3%-49.8%), indicating at least one clinically relevant error in about half of cases. Treatment planning was the only endpoint differing between models after Holm-Bonferroni correction, favoring Gemini 3.0 (OR, 1.457; adjusted p = .003). Conclusions Both models performed acceptably on individual endpoints and common presentations, but performance was endpoint-specific and substantially reduced on integrated assessment and low-prevalence categories. These findings support use of LLMs in endodontic diagnosis and treatment planning as adjunctive tools, but not without expert supervision.

title: Comparison of the efficacy of three-dimensional printing-assisted strategy and traditional total ankle arthroplasty in the treatment of end-stage ankle arthritis.
abstract: Objective To compare perioperative parameters, early functional outcomes, and complication profiles between 3D printing-assisted total ankle arthroplasty strategy incorporating preoperative virtual planning, patient-specific osteotomy guides, and a customized talar component and conventional total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) in the treatment of end-stage ankle arthritis. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on data from 44 patients diagnosed with end-stage ankle arthritis who were admitted to our hospital between January 2021 and December 2023. Among them, 20 patients (observation group) underwent total ankle arthroplasty (TAA) using a 3D-printed patient-specific TAA strategy, while 24 patients (control group) received conventional TAA using the same tibial component and polyethylene liner but a standard off-the-shelf talar component, together with standard instrumentation. The following parameters were recorded and evaluated: operative duration, intraoperative blood loss, length of postoperative hospital stay, intraoperative fluoroscopy time, preoperative and postoperative American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) scores, visual analogue scale (VAS) scores, and ankle range of motion (ROM). Additionally, the occurrence of soft tissue-related complications was monitored. Results The AOFAS score, VAS score, and ankle range of motion (ROM) in both groups showed significant improvement postoperatively compared to preoperative values (P < 0.05). However, no statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups (P > 0.05). With regard to surgical outcomes, including operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative hospitalization duration, and the intraoperative fluoroscopy time, the observation group demonstrated significantly better results than the control group (P < 0.001). Concerning postoperative complications, the observation group experienced only one case of superficial infection, whereas the control group had two cases of superficial infection and one case of wound edge necrosis. Although the total complication rate was slightly lower in the observation group, the difference between the two groups was not statistically significant (P = 0.389). Postoperative radiographic analysis confirmed significantly improved alignment accuracy of the tibial component in the observation group compared to the control group (P < 0.05). Conclusion The 3D printing-assisted TAA strategy appears to improve perioperative efficiency and short-term radiographic alignment accuracy compared with conventional TAA, whereas short-term functional outcomes and wound-related complication rates remain comparable between groups. Given the additional preoperative preparation time and cost, its theoretical promise for patients with complex deformities and its potential effect on long-term implant survival require further confirmation through prospective, randomized studies with long-term follow-up.

title: Deep learning-based spot weight generation for online adaptive IMPT: implementation and technical feasibility on a clinical delivery system.
abstract: Purpose To investigate the feasibility of a deep learning-based method for generating intensity-modulated proton therapy (IMPT) spot weights to enable a faster, more automated workflow. Methods A 3D Attention U-Net with a masked mean absolute error loss generated spot weights from four input channels (optimized plan dose, reference dose, CT image, spot mask), using planned spot weights as labels, and trained and tested on prostate, brain, and lung cases. Robustness was evaluated on target dose metrics only. The workflow was validated in the Eclipse® treatment planning system and delivered on a ProBeam 360° system. Results For weights in the range 0-5, mean absolute errors were below 0.8 for the prostate and brain models (15.9% and 48.1% of all weights, respectively) and below 1.7 for the lung model (31.2%). Mean relative errors were below 10% for the prostate model (5-65, 83.7%), 20% for the brain model (5-65, 51.7%), and 40% for the lung model (5-110, 68.6%); the remaining weights lay above these ranges and accounted for <0.5% of all weights. Gamma passing rates within the body contours (2%, 2 mm, 10% dose threshold) were 99.73 ± 0.32%, 98.95 ± 0.86%, and 92.75 ± 3.52% for the prostate, brain, and lung models, respectively. All delivered plans met the clinical QA acceptance criteria. Conclusion The proposed framework demonstrates the technical feasibility of generating IMPT spot weights with deep learning and implementing them on a clinical delivery system. Further improvement is needed for heterogeneous sites such as the lung.

title: Uncertainty quantification for detecting out-of-distribution cases in deep learning segmentation of head and neck organs of interest.
abstract: Purpose Quality assurance (QA) of auto-segmentations is necessary for safe clinical deployment. Deep learning models are optimised for data similar to their training set, but reliability drops with out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. This study evaluates whether uncertainty quantification (UQ) can detect OOD inputs arising from distribution shift in head and neck organ of interest (OOI) auto-segmentation. Materials and methods Monte Carlo dropout-based uncertainty scores and geometric accuracy of nnU-Net models were evaluated in two experiments. First, as a proof-of-concept, we assessed whether uncertainty scores detect metal artefact (N = 10) from non-artefact cases (N = 10) on a baseline model (mixed training data, N = 620) and a no-metal model (artefact-free training data, N = 620). Second, in a clinically realistic experiment, we split a fine-tuning dataset by uncertainty score to obtain a narrow model (low-uncertainty cases, N = 21) and a broad model (high-uncertainty cases, N = 21). A held-out test set (N = 76) evaluated whether segmentation accuracy differed between uncertainty categories. Results Both experiments showed that uncertainty scores reflect the learned training distribution. In the supervised experiment, the no-metal model demonstrated greater uncertainty score separation between artefact and non-artefact cases (1.1 × 10 5 vs 0.6 × 10 5 ) than the baseline model (1.1 × 10 5 vs 0.8 × 10 5 ). In the unsupervised experiment, the narrow model performed significantly better on certain than uncertain cases (p = 0.04), while no difference was seen for the broad model (p = 0.34), which did include these cases in training. Conclusions Uncertainty quantification can detect distribution shifts in radiotherapy auto-segmentation. This could support automated QA workflows by identifying in-distribution cases and enabling the application of specialised models.

title: Imaging And Outcomes In The Treatment Of Sacral Dural Arteriovenous Fistulas.
abstract: Objective Spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas (DAVFs) in the sacral region are extremely rare and their intradural retrograde draining system has not been investigated in detail. The aim of this study was to characterize the venous drainage patterns of sacral DAVFs based on our clinical experience in treating patients with this condition. Methods We retrospectively reviewed the clinical data of patients with sacral DAVFs treated at our institution from January 2016 to January 2024. Preoperative spinal angiography was used to evaluate the positional relationship between the shunt point of sacral DAVF and the vertebral midline. We proposed that if the location of the shunt point was located on the midline, the draining vein would be the filum terminale vein (FTV); if the shunt point was located off the midline, the draining vein would be the radiculomedullary vein (RMV). Results A total of 17 sacral DAVFs patients treated with direct surgery were included in this study. All patients presented with lower extremity weakness and numbness. Sphincter dysfunction was present in 15 patients (88.2%). The mean interval from symptom onset to diagnosis was 14.1 months (range 1-96 months). Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging(MRI) detected T2 hyperintensity at the level of the conus medullaris and intradural flow voids in all patients. Spinal angiography confirmed the diagnosis of sacral DAVF in all cases, and complete fistula occlusion was achieved with surgical ligation in all patients. Intraoperatively, 4 patients with the midline location of the shunt point were confirmed to have FTV as the draining vein, while the other 13 patients with off-midline shunt point were confirmed to have RMV as the draining vein. The intraoperative findings were completely consistent with the preoperative assessment of the draining veins based on the location of the shunt point. Conclusions The draining veins of sacral DAVFs are not always the FTVs, in fact, most sacral DAVFs drain via the RMV. With our simple imaging-based method, the two different types of draining veins in sacral DAVFs can be preliminarily identified before surgery.

title: Degenerative cervical myelopathy: early detection and the potential for preventing disability.
abstract: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM), the most common non-traumatic spinal cord injury, is a prevalent, progressive, and highly disabling neurological disease, causing heterogeneous impairment ranging from sensory loss and impaired hand dexterity to gait, balance, and autonomic dysfunction. Disability often persists despite surgical decompression, and untreated disease can progress to irreversible neurological injury, including tetraplegia. Current clinical management is largely reactive, with diagnosis and intervention typically only after neurological deterioration has become clinically apparent and radiographic evidence of cervical myelopathy is established. Advances in multimodal diagnostics over the past 5 years are now enabling the detection of subtle spinal cord injury, biological disease activity, and subclinical neurodegeneration before overt clinical disability. Quantitative spinal cord MRI, advanced neurophysiological assessments, dynamic biomechanical metrics, and sensitive functional testing provide complementary tools for early detection, risk stratification, and prognostication. Together, these approaches are redefining DCM as a disease that should be managed proactively. Evidence supports decompressive surgery in patients with moderate-to-severe disease, whereas in milder disease or in spinal stenosis that might develop into DCM, the management of patients should be interdisciplinary, with active surveillance to detect early deterioration or decompressive surgery in selected cases. Improved prediction of disease trajectories and clearer evidence on long-term outcomes could enable selective earlier intervention and help to prevent neurological disability.

title: Pulmonary nodules: classification, biomarkers, signaling pathways, diseases, early diagnosis and management.
abstract: Pulmonary nodules are increasingly detected by thoracic imaging and low-dose computed tomography-based lung cancer screening, but most are benign, transient, or indolent. Clinically, the key task is to distinguish nodules that require timely cancer-directed evaluation from those that can be safely observed. This review summarizes the classification, disease spectrum, risk assessment, early diagnosis, biomarkers, signaling mechanisms, translational models, and management of pulmonary nodules. We first distinguish imaging phenotypes and disease entities, then differentiate the individual-level models used to select candidates for lung cancer screening from the nodule-level models and structured reporting systems used after nodule detection. Low-dose computed tomography remains the foundation of screening and surveillance approaches, whereas magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography, contrast-enhanced computed tomography, nonsurgical biopsy, surgical diagnosis, and local therapies play more selective roles depending on the probability of malignancy and patient fitness. Noninvasive biomarkers, including circulating cellular, nucleic acid, methylation, protein, autoantibody, extracellular vesicle, and metabolic analytes, are most likely to serve as adjuncts to imaging and clinical risk assessment rather than as stand-alone diagnostic tests. Artificial intelligence may support detection, workflow efficiency, malignancy risk reclassification, invasiveness assessment, and multimodal integration, but its value depends on external validation, calibration, implementation, and prospective evidence of management benefit. Mechanistic studies of adenocarcinoma spectrum subsolid nodules have implicated the involvement of early oncogenic signaling, genomic instability, immune escape, stromal and vascular remodeling, and adaptive survival pathways. Translational models can support mechanistic and procedural research, but do not replicate real-world nodule management in patients. Overall, care for pulmonary nodules should be risk-adapted, longitudinal, multidisciplinary, and patient-centered.

title: AEGIS: an operational infrastructure for post-market governance of adaptive medical AI under US and EU regulatory frameworks.
abstract: Medical AI requires governance preserving safety during continuous improvement. FDA Predetermined Change Control Plans (PCCP) and EU post-market surveillance address iterative updates but lack operational tooling. We present AEGIS, an internal governance and post-market-monitoring infrastructure designed to support the documentation of predetermined governance pathways for PCCP and Medical Devices Regulation alignment. AEGIS comprises dataset assimilation and retraining, model monitoring, and conditional decision-making modules. It utilizes a four-category taxonomy (APPROVE, CONDITIONAL APPROVAL, CLINICAL REVIEW, REJECT) and an independent ALARM signal. Instantiating AEGIS for sepsis prediction (PhysioNet) and brain-tumor segmentation (BraTS) exercised all decision categories, successfully routing failures to the critical REJECT + ALARM state (no deployable model; released model at risk). On real cross-site data, drift detection ROC-AUC rose from 0.82 to 1.00, reliably triggering near 500-patient batches with zero false alarms. This proof-of-concept utilizes illustrative clinical models; drift scoring quantifies covariate shift only, leaving concept drift for future work.
